sections.title: ABUSI Reliable Change
sections.text:
A change of 7 points or more in either direction is treated as reliable, meaning it is larger than would be expected from measurement error. A decrease of that size indicates a reliable reduction in the urge, and an increase indicates a reliable worsening. The threshold was established across a full course of treatment, so change over a single week is worth reading with more caution.
On repeat administration the report compares the current score with the initial administration, and from the third administration onward also with the immediately previous one, giving each comparison its own reliable change result. A change in severity category is reported against the initial administration only, so a client whose score moves back and forth across one boundary does not receive a category-change sentence every session.

sections.title: ABUSI Risk Alert
sections.text:
Two response options carry clinical significance regardless of the total score. On item 4 (how difficult it was to resist), the highest option, Was not able to resist, indicates that the client could not resist the urge during the week. On item 2 (how strong the urge was at its most severe point), the highest option, Strong urge and would have self-injured if able to, indicates that only the absence of opportunity stood between the urge and the behaviour.
When item 4 is answered Was not able to resist, the report displays a red alert beneath the results table and a Safety Risk Alert tag is added to the results dashboard. When either response is given, the interpretive text includes a Risk of Self-Harm or Suicide paragraph naming the item or items endorsed, with a recommendation to follow suicide risk assessment protocols to determine the nature, severity, and immediacy of the risk. Moderate and Severe results also carry a coloured severity tag.

sections.title: ABUSI Graphs
sections.text:
On first administration, a bar chart displays the total score against a background shaded by the severity categories, with a right-hand strip marking the 50th, 75th, 80th, 85th, and 90th NSSI Treatment Percentiles. A score of 0 sits in an unshaded strip at the foot of the chart labelled None Reported.

On repeat administration, a line chart plots the total score across all administrations against the same bands and percentile markers, so the trajectory of the urge over treatment can be seen at a glance.

sections.title: Development of the ABUSI
sections.text: The ABUSI was developed at the Alexian Brothers Behavioral Health Hospital and first validated in 386 adolescents and adults admitted to its Self-Injury Recovery Services programme between 2007 and 2009 (Washburn et al., 2010). The sample was 90.7% female and 86.3% non-Hispanic white, aged 11 to 61, and mostly adolescents (64.9%). Items were adapted from the 5-item Penn Alcohol Craving Scale by changing the content from alcohol craving to the urge to self-injure. Completion was high, with 95.6% of patients answering all five items.

sections.title: ABUSI Reliability
sections.text:
Internal consistency is high. In the development sample, Cronbach’s alpha was .92 at admission and .96 at discharge, and all five items correlated highly with the total ( r = .87 to .92; Washburn et al., 2010). Similar values have been reported in later samples from the same service: .93 in 1,502 adolescents and young adults (Victor et al., 2015), .93 in 1,780 patients (Victor et al., 2016), and .92 in 1,327 day-treatment patients (Slesinger et al., 2021).
Test-retest reliability over 48 hours was high for the total score (ICC = .84, n = 46), ranging from .60 for the duration item to .83 for the frequency item (Washburn et al., 2010). The short interval means this describes stability over about a day rather than over the one-week period the measure asks about.

sections.title: ABUSI Factor Structure
sections.text: Exploratory factor analysis identified a single factor, severity of the urge to self-injure, accounting for 70.6% of the variance, with loadings from .76 (duration) to .92 (overall urge; Washburn et al., 2010). A confirmatory factor analysis of the Spanish adaptation in 752 Colombian adolescents supported the same single-factor solution (Bahamón et al., 2023). No confirmatory analysis has been conducted on the English version. The ABUSI is scored as a single total.

sections.title: ABUSI Validity
sections.text:
Convergent validity. Total scores correlated positively with self-injury frequency, suicidal ideation, and functional impairment, and negatively with quality of life and satisfaction ( r = −.48 at admission; Washburn et al., 2010).
Known-groups validity. Among 511 patients admitted for self-injury treatment, those meeting the proposed DSM-5 criteria for non-suicidal self-injury disorder scored higher than those who did not (21.06 compared with 16.83; d = 0.52; Washburn et al., 2015). In 1,502 adolescents and young adults, urge severity was substantially higher among those reporting past-week suicidal ideation ( d = 1.16), a larger difference than for any other self-injury characteristic examined (Victor et al., 2015).
Predictive and incremental validity. Each additional point at admission was associated with higher odds of re-admission ( OR = 1.06, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.11) and lower odds of clinically significant improvement in quality of life by discharge ( OR = 0.97, 95% CI 0.94 to 0.99), and admission scores improved the prediction of self-injury frequency at discharge over and above baseline frequency, age, and gender (Washburn et al., 2010). In 1,327 day-treatment patients, stronger urges at admission predicted less improvement in self-injury frequency (Slesinger et al., 2021).
Comparison with other measures. A systematic review of 11 instruments measuring NSSI in adolescents found the ABUSI among the two best-evidenced (Chávez-Flores et al., 2019), and an evidence-based review of brief, free youth mental health measures rated its psychometrics excellent, the only one of six suicidality measures to receive the highest rating (Becker-Haimes et al., 2020).

sections.title: ABUSI Sensitivity to Change
sections.text:
Responsiveness to treatment is the strongest area of the ABUSI evidence base. Among 277 patients with admission and discharge data, total scores fell from 18.47 to 11.84, a within-group effect size of 0.83, the largest of the outcome measures administered alongside it and the only one on which average change exceeded its reliable change threshold (Washburn et al., 2010). Among 923 day-treatment patients, scores fell by 3.6 to 4.1 points on average (effect sizes 0.47 to 0.52; Washburn et al., 2023). In 1,780 patients, reductions in the reported functions of self-injury were no longer significant once change in urge severity was accounted for, suggesting the urge captures much of what changes in treatment (Victor et al., 2016).
In 43 patients later re-admitted, scores fell from admission to discharge, rose between discharge and re-admission, and did not differ between the two admissions, the pattern expected if the measure tracks clinical state (Washburn et al., 2010).
The published reliable change cutoff is 6.58, which NovoPsych rounds to 7. It reproduces from the scale’s internal consistency rather than its test-retest reliability, and the authors applied it to change between admission and discharge, so it is best suited to comparisons across a course of treatment.

sections.title: ABUSI Normative Data
sections.text: No community norms exist for the ABUSI. The NSSI Treatment Percentile is calculated by NovoPsych from a single clinical sample of 1,327 adolescents and adults admitted for partial hospitalisation or intensive outpatient treatment of NSSI, who scored 18.4 (SD 8.0) at admission (Washburn et al., 2023). That sample was 87.4% female and 75.3% non-Hispanic white. The average closely matches the development sample a decade earlier (18.02, SD 8.45; Washburn et al., 2010), supporting the stability of the reference point, and clients reporting self-injurious disordered eating scored higher than those presenting with self-injury alone (21.3 compared with 17.2; Washburn et al., 2023).

sections.title: What is the difference between measuring the urge to self-injure and measuring self-injury itself?
sections.text: They answer different questions. Counting episodes of self-injury tells you what a person did, while measuring the urge tells you what they experienced and had to manage. Someone may go a week without self-injuring while experiencing frequent and intense urges throughout, and that week is clinically quite different from one in which the urge never arose, even though the behavioural count is the same. Higher urges at admission have also been found to predict self-injury frequency at discharge after accounting for how often the person was self-injuring at admission, which makes the urge worth monitoring alongside the behaviour.

sections.title: Does a score of zero mean the person is not at risk?
sections.text: No. A score of zero means the client reported no urge to self-injure during the seven days the measure asks about. Among adolescents and adults admitted for treatment of self-injury, roughly one in eight reported no urge in the week before admission, so a zero is not unusual even in a population receiving intensive treatment. It is best read as information about that particular week rather than a general statement about the presence or absence of self-injury concerns.

sections.title: The percentile compares my client with people in treatment for self-injury. How should I interpret that?
sections.text: With the comparison group in mind. Because everyone in the reference sample was admitted for treatment of NSSI, a client can score well below that group and still be reporting urges that are clinically relevant. This is why the severity category, which is based on what the response options themselves describe, is the primary basis for interpretation. The percentile adds context about how the client compares with a treatment population and should be read alongside the severity category, the individual item responses, and the broader clinical picture.

sections.title: How much change on the ABUSI is meaningful?
sections.text: A change of 7 points or more, in either direction, is larger than would be expected from the natural variability of the measure and can be treated as a real change. Smaller changes do not meet this threshold, although they may still be clinically meaningful. Average improvement across a whole treatment programme is sometimes smaller than 7 points, so a client who does not reach that level of improvement is not necessarily making no progress.

sections.title: Is the ABUSI a screening tool for self-injury?
sections.text: It was not designed as one, and its total score does not indicate whether a person is or is not engaging in NSSI. The measure assumes self-injury is already known or suspected, and its questions are phrased accordingly. Its established use is tracking the intensity of the urge to self-injure over time, with the individual item responses adding detail about the frequency, intensity, duration, and controllability of those urges.

sections.title: What does the ABUSI add when a client is already being asked about self-harm in session?
sections.text: It gives a consistent, quantified record of urges that can be compared across administrations, and it separates the urge into its component parts. Two clients with similar totals may differ substantially in whether their urges are frequent but manageable or rare but overwhelming, and those patterns suggest different clinical priorities. Having the same five questions answered each week also makes gradual change visible in a way that recall in session often does not.

assessment.name: Why Have Sex? Questionnaire Short Form (YSEX-SF)
assessment.description: The Why Have Sex? Questionnaire Short Form (YSEX-SF) is a 28-item self-report measure of sexual motivation for adults aged 18 years and over (Meston et al., 2020). It assesses the reasons a person has engaged in sex, capturing how frequently each of 14 distinct motivations has led them to have sexual intercourse across their past sexual experiences. For respondents who have not previously had sex, the measure instead assesses the likelihood that each motivation would lead them to have sex.

administration.instructions: People have sex (i.e., sexual intercourse) for many different reasons. Below is a list of some of these reasons. Please indicate how frequently each of the following reasons led you to have sex in the past. If you have not had sex in the past, use the scale to indicate the likelihood that each of the following reasons would lead you to have sex. I have had sex in the past because… Response scale (same for every item): 1 = None of my sexual experiences; 2 = A few of my sexual experiences; 3 = Some of my sexual experiences; 4 = Many of my sexual experiences; 5 = All of my sexual experiences.

source_rule_excerpts: Internal consistency was assessed in a validation sample of 223 United States adults recruited online (ages 19 to 76, median 33; Meston et al., 2020, Study 2). The two-item subscale alphas ranged from .42 to .93, with an average of .74. Reliability was strongest for Reproduction (α = .93), Mate Guarding (α = .82), Resources (α = .81), Stress Reduction (α = .80), and Physical Desirability (α = .80), and acceptable for most remaining subscales, including Love and Commitment (α = .78), Social Status (α = .76), Experience Seeking (α = .75), Duty/Pressure (α = .75), Self-Esteem Boost (α = .74), and Revenge (α = .70). Pleasure (α = .68) and Expression (α = .62) showed more modest internal consistency, and Practical was the weakest subscale (α = .42), reflecting its two items spanning distinct physical and emotional benefits.

source_guidance.title: YSEX-SF Scoring
source_guidance.text:
All 28 items have response options ranging from 1 (None of my sexual experiences) to 5 (All of my sexual experiences). Each of the 14 subscales is scored by summing its two items, giving subscale scores from 2 to 10. Higher scores indicate that a greater proportion of the respondent’s sexual experiences have been motivated by that reason.
No total score is computed, and the measure has no norms, percentiles, or clinical cut-offs. The clinical output is the 14-subscale profile. For respondents who have not had sex, the instructions direct them to rate the likelihood that each reason would lead them to have sex, and their profile is read as anticipated rather than experienced motivation.
Subscale | Items | What it assesses
Stress Reduction | 1, 15 | Sex used to release frustration, anxiety, or stress. Higher scores may indicate that sex serves an emotion-regulation function.
Pleasure | 2, 16 | Sex motivated by physical enjoyment and desire. Typically among the most frequently endorsed motivations.
Physical Desirability | 3, 17 | Sex motivated by attraction to the other person’s appearance. The items refer to the person rather than a partner, reflecting that the measure covers casual and non-partnered sex.
Experience Seeking | 4, 18 | Sex pursued for novelty, adventure, or excitement.
Resources | 5, 19 | Sex exchanged for tangible gain such as money or favours. Elevated scores indicate that exchange-based motivations feature in the respondent’s experiences.
Reproduction | 6, 20 | Sex motivated by the desire to conceive. Scores are strongly context-dependent and interpreted in light of life stage and relationship circumstances.
Social Status | 7, 21 | Sex used to enhance reputation or standing.
Revenge | 8, 22 | Sex used to retaliate against a partner or get even with someone. Elevated scores may indicate unresolved relational conflict.
Practical | 9, 23 | Sex pursued for practical benefits. The two items span distinct content, one physical and one emotional, so reviewing them individually shows which is driving the score.
Love and Commitment | 10, 24 | Sex used to express love and feel connected. Low scores in a partnered respondent may be clinically informative about the relational function of sex.
Expression | 11, 25 | Sex used to mark special occasions or transitions, such as welcomes, farewells, and celebrations.
Self-Esteem Boost | 12, 26 | Sex used to feel better about oneself. Elevated scores may indicate that sexual activity is serving a self-worth regulation function.
Duty/Pressure | 13, 27 | Sex engaged in out of obligation or in response to pressure. Elevated scores can reflect experiences of sexual coercion.
Mate Guarding | 14, 28 | Sex used to keep a partner from straying. Elevated scores may indicate relationship insecurity or fear of abandonment.

source_guidance.title: Interpreting the YSEX-SF Profile
source_guidance.text:
The profile is interpreted relatively. The most clinically informative feature is which motivations are most and least frequent for the respondent, rather than the value of any single subscale in isolation. Considered together, the 14 subscale scores describe the overall shape of the respondent’s motivational profile.
Conceptually related subscales are often more informative in combination than any subscale considered alone. Representative examples include:
Frequent Duty/Pressure alongside frequent Mate Guarding may indicate that sex is functioning to preserve a relationship in which the person feels insecure, directing attention toward relational safety and communication.
Frequent Stress Reduction alongside frequent Self-Esteem Boost may indicate that sex is serving an emotion-regulation or self-worth function.
Frequent Pleasure, Love and Commitment, and Expression together describe sexual activity that is intrinsically and relationally motivated.
Infrequent Pleasure or Love and Commitment in a partnered respondent presenting with sexual dissatisfaction may itself be the clinically salient finding.

source_guidance.title: YSEX-SF Norms
source_guidance.text: NovoPsych does not calculate YSEX-SF percentiles. The only available normative data come from the validation sample of 223 United States adults recruited online, reported separately by gender, with pronounced floor effects on several subscales because most respondents endorse None of my sexual experiences for motivations such as Resources, Revenge, and Reproduction. Percentiles derived from that sample would imply a reference comparison and a degree of precision the data do not support. The measure also has no clinical cut-offs anywhere in the literature. Interpretation therefore rests on the frequency descriptors and the shape of the profile.

source_guidance.title: Should clinicians focus on the highest-scoring subscale?
source_guidance.text: Not necessarily. The pattern across subscales is often more informative than any single score. Most people report a combination of motivations rather than a single dominant reason, and results are best interpreted alongside the client’s history, presenting concerns, and broader clinical assessment.

context_sections.title: Why Have Sex? Questionnaire Short Form (YSEX-SF)
context_sections.text:
The Why Have Sex? Questionnaire Short Form (YSEX-SF) is a 28-item self-report measure of sexual motivation for adults aged 18 years and over (Meston et al., 2020). It assesses the reasons a person has engaged in sex, capturing how frequently each of 14 distinct motivations has led them to have sexual intercourse across their past sexual experiences. For respondents who have not previously had sex, the measure instead assesses the likelihood that each motivation would lead them to have sex.
5 minutes
Ages 18+
Formulation
Administer Now

context_sections.title: How could understanding someone's reasons for having sex be helpful in therapy?
context_sections.text: Sexual difficulties can sometimes be better understood once the motivations behind sexual behaviour are considered. Two clients with identical presentations, for example low desire, can have very different profiles: one may have sex mainly out of obligation and relationship insecurity, while the other’s profile centres on pleasure and connection that has recently declined. The YSEX-SF makes these patterns more explicit, helping the clinician and client build a shared formulation of what role sex plays in the client’s life and identify areas that may warrant further exploration.

context_sections.title: Is there a right or wrong reason to have sex?
context_sections.text:
No. The research behind the YSEX-SF identified over two hundred distinct reasons people have sex, spanning pleasure, love, curiosity, comfort, celebration, and many others, and most people endorse a mix. The measure describes how frequently each motivation has featured in the respondent’s experiences without judging any of them as necessarily positive or negative.
Some patterns may still warrant further clinical exploration. Sex motivated primarily by distress reduction or self-esteem enhancement may suggest an opportunity to explore broader coping strategies or emotional functioning.

context_sections.title: What does it mean if Duty/Pressure is among a client's most endorsed reasons?
context_sections.text: Frequent sex out of obligation or pressure can range from consensual but unwanted sex within a relationship through to experiences of sexual coercion. The NovoPsych report flags elevated Duty/Pressure scores for the clinician, and follow-up may be warranted: clarifying who or what the pressure comes from, whether it is current or historical, and how the client feels about these experiences. Depending on what emerges, treatment might focus on relational communication and consent, assertiveness, or processing past experiences.

context_sections.title: How does the YSEX-SF relate to the original YSEX? instrument?
context_sections.text: The original YSEX? contains over 140 items and was developed as a comprehensive research taxonomy of sexual motivation. The YSEX-SF was created by the same authors, who selected or wrote the two most representative items for each motivational domain, reducing completion time substantially while retaining the structure of the original. Scores on the short form correlate strongly with their long-form counterparts. The short form also introduced one new subscale, Reproduction, and renamed the Utilitarian subscale to Practical.

context_sections.title: Can someone complete the YSEX-SF if they have not had sex?
context_sections.text: Yes. The instructions ask respondents who have not had sex to rate how likely each reason would be to lead them to have sex. Their profile reflects anticipated rather than experienced motivation, which can still be clinically useful, for example in work with clients who are anxious about sexual relationships or exploring their readiness for them.

context_sections.title: Should clinicians focus on the highest-scoring subscale?
context_sections.text: Not necessarily. The pattern across subscales is often more informative than any single score. Most people report a combination of motivations rather than a single dominant reason, and results are best interpreted alongside the client’s history, presenting concerns, and broader clinical assessment.

context_sections.title: YSEX-SF Overview
context_sections.text:
People have sex for far more varied reasons than the familiar ones of pleasure, procreation, and love. The research programme behind the instrument identified 237 distinct reasons (Meston & Buss, 2007). Which of these motivations drive a person’s sexual behaviour carries meaningful information about their sexual desire, relationships, and wellbeing, and making those motivations explicit gives clinicians a structured way to understand what underlies a client’s sexual behaviour.
YSEX-SF Example Item

context_sections.title: YSEX-SF Subscales
context_sections.text:
The 14 subscales span physical, emotional, goal-oriented, and insecurity-related motivations for sex. Each is measured by two items.
Stress Reduction : sex used to release frustration, anxiety, or stress.
Pleasure : sex motivated by physical enjoyment and desire.
Physical Desirability : sex motivated by attraction to the other person’s appearance.
Experience Seeking : sex pursued for novelty, adventure, or excitement.
Resources : sex exchanged for tangible gain such as money or favours.
Reproduction : sex motivated by the desire to conceive.
Social Status : sex used to enhance reputation or standing.
Revenge : sex used to retaliate against a partner or get even with someone.
Practical : sex pursued for practical physical or emotional benefits.
Love and Commitment : sex used to express love and feel connected.
Expression : sex used to mark special occasions or transitions.
Self-Esteem Boost : sex used to feel better about oneself.
Duty/Pressure : sex engaged in out of obligation or in response to pressure.
Mate Guarding : sex used to keep a partner from straying.

context_sections.title: Clinical Applications of the YSEX-SF
context_sections.text:
The YSEX-SF was originally developed for research on sexual motivation and remains suited to that purpose. On NovoPsych it is applied clinically, chiefly to support formulation and feedback, rather than screening, diagnosis, or progress monitoring.
The measure can be used in sex therapy, relationship counselling, and general clinical practice wherever a client’s sexual behaviour, desire, or satisfaction is a focus of treatment. Its primary contribution is to formulation: the 14-subscale profile answers the question of what is driving a client’s sexual behaviour. A profile dominated by Duty/Pressure and Mate Guarding motivations tells a fundamentally different clinical story from one dominated by Pleasure and Love and Commitment motivations. The pattern of motivations across a profile can also clarify presentations involving mismatched desire, sexual dissatisfaction, or relationship insecurity.
The YSEX-SF supports psychoeducation and feedback conversations. The research behind the instrument documented a far wider range of sexual motivations than is typically assumed, and reviewing the profile collaboratively as part of treatment can normalise a client’s experience and open conversations that might not otherwise arise.
The measure provides a snapshot of the respondent’s motivational history rather than a measure of change over time. It functions closer to a structured screening of motivations than to an outcome measure, and is best used for formulation and feedback at a given point in care.

context_sections.title: YSEX-SF Frequency Descriptors
context_sections.text:
Each subscale score is accompanied by a frequency descriptor taken directly from the measure’s own response options. Because each subscale consists of two items scored from 1 (None of my sexual experiences) to 5 (All of my sexual experiences), the summed subscale score can be translated back into the corresponding response scale to aid interpretation. These descriptors are not part of the original scoring system, and provide a plain-language summary of how frequently each motivation has contributed to the respondent’s sexual experiences.
Subscale score | Frequency descriptor
2 | None of my sexual experiences
3 to 4 | A few of my sexual experiences
5 to 6 | Some of my sexual experiences
7 to 8 | Many of my sexual experiences
9 to 10 | All of my sexual experiences
These descriptors are frequency labels rather than severity ratings or indicators of clinical significance. The clinical relevance of a given descriptor depends on the motivation being assessed and the respondent’s circumstances. A descriptor of Many of my sexual experiences may be expected for motivations such as Pleasure or Love and Commitment, whereas the same descriptor for Duty/Pressure may warrant further clinical exploration regarding possible coercion or unwanted sexual experiences.

context_sections.text:
The profile is interpreted relatively. The most clinically informative feature is which motivations are most and least frequent for the respondent, rather than the value of any single subscale in isolation. context_sections.title: Elevated Duty/Pressure
context_sections.text:
The Duty/Pressure items (I was pressured into doing it and I felt obligated to) can reflect experiences of sexual coercion. Where either item is endorsed above None of my sexual experiences, the report displays a note for the clinician showing both item responses, and adds a Duty/Pressure tag to the results dashboard. Clinicians are encouraged to review the individual item responses directly and follow up carefully to clarify the nature and context of these experiences.
Duty/Pressure is deliberately the only subscale carrying an automated clinician note. Elevations on Resources or Revenge can also carry clinical weight, but their meaning is more context-dependent, and they are left to the profile text and clinician review so the single high-stakes flag is not diluted.

context_sections.title: YSEX-SF Graphs
context_sections.text:
The report presents a horizontal bar chart of the 14 subscale scores, one bar per subscale, in a fixed order on an axis from 2 to 10. Five shaded vertical bands behind the bars mark the frequency-descriptor regions (None, A few, Some, Many, and All), deepening in shade from left to right, so each bar’s length can be read as its frequency descriptor and the overall shape of the profile is visible at a glance.

The chart shows the profile for the current administration. Repeat administrations regenerate the single-administration profile. No longitudinal score-tracking graphs are produced, consistent with the measure’s snapshot design.

context_sections.title: Development of the YSEX-SF
context_sections.text:
The original taxonomy for the 142-item YSEX? was developed in two stages (Meston & Buss, 2007). First, 444 participants nominated reasons for having sex, producing 237 distinct reasons. The long-form instrument demonstrated strong internal consistency, with alphas exceeding .85 for each factor score.
The YSEX-SF was developed by Meston and colleagues from this same dataset (Meston et al., 2020, Study 1). The two most representative items for each subscale were selected using the original factor loadings combined with structured consensus judgements of conceptual fit. Where the original items were too specific to represent a subscale in two items, broader composite items were written. Meston, personal communication, July 22, 2026). This is how NovoPsych presents it.

context_sections.title: YSEX-SF Reliability
context_sections.text:
Internal consistency was assessed in a validation sample of 223 United States adults recruited online (ages 19 to 76, median 33; Meston et al., 2020, Study 2). The two-item subscale alphas ranged from .42 to .93, with an average of .74. Reliability was strongest for Reproduction (α = .93), Mate Guarding (α = .82), Resources (α = .81), Stress Reduction (α = .80), and Physical Desirability (α = .80), and acceptable for most remaining subscales, including Love and Commitment (α = .78), Social Status (α = .76), Experience Seeking (α = .75), Duty/Pressure (α = .75), Self-Esteem Boost (α = .74), and Revenge (α = .70). Pleasure (α = .68) and Expression (α = .62) showed more modest internal consistency, and Practical was the weakest subscale (α = .42), reflecting its two items spanning distinct physical and emotional benefits.
Because Cronbach’s alpha rises with the number of items, two-item subscales tend to produce lower coefficients than longer scales. These values should be read with the short scale length in mind rather than as evidence of weak items.

context_sections.title: YSEX-SF Factor Structure
context_sections.text:
A confirmatory factor analysis in the validation sample (N = 218) supported the 14-factor structure, with acceptable model fit (CFI = 0.91, TLI = 0.86, RMSEA = 0.070, 90% CI [0.061, 0.078]) and standardised item loadings ranging from .52 to .92, excluding the variance-constrained Reproduction item whose corrected loading is reported as 1.00. context_sections.title: YSEX-SF Validity
context_sections.text:
Cross-form validity between the YSEX-SF and the full-length YSEX? was generally strong (Meston et al., 2020, Study 2). Twelve of the 14 subscales correlated between r = .61 and r = .85 with their long-form counterparts. The Practical subscale correlated moderately with the long-form Utilitarian subscale (r = .43), reflecting the substantial condensing of that subscale’s content, and the new Reproduction subscale correlated moderately with the long-form Resources subscale from which its items were drawn (r = .39), consistent with its deliberate isolation as a distinct construct.
Construct validity was supported by theoretically coherent associations with personality and sexual-strategy measures. Higher scores on all three Dark Triad traits (Machiavellianism, narcissism, and psychopathy) were associated with more frequent Social Status, Revenge, and Mate Guarding motivations in both men and women. Love and Commitment showed no association with any Dark Triad trait in either gender, supporting the discriminant validity of the profile. Sociosexual orientation (openness to uncommitted sex) was associated with more frequent Revenge motivations in both genders, and with less frequent Love and Commitment motivation in women.

context_sections.title: YSEX-SF Gender Comparisons
context_sections.text: Gender differences on the YSEX-SF were small. Men scored higher than women on the three largest differences in motivation: Physical Desirability (d = 0.37), Social Status (d = 0.35), and Experience Seeking (d = 0.33). The largest difference on which women scored higher was Love and Commitment (d = 0.27). None of these differences remained statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons (Meston et al., 2020). Scores are therefore interpreted without reference to gender.

context_sections.title: YSEX-SF Norms
context_sections.text: NovoPsych does not calculate YSEX-SF percentiles. The only available normative data come from the validation sample of 223 United States adults recruited online, reported separately by gender, with pronounced floor effects on several subscales because most respondents endorse None of my sexual experiences for motivations such as Resources, Revenge, and Reproduction. Percentiles derived from that sample would imply a reference comparison and a degree of precision the data do not support. The measure also has no clinical cut-offs anywhere in the literature. Interpretation therefore rests on the frequency descriptors and the shape of the profile.

context_sections.title: Why Have Sex? Questionnaire Short Form (YSEX-SF)
context_sections.text:
The Why Have Sex? Questionnaire Short Form (YSEX-SF) is a 28-item self-report measure of sexual motivation for adults aged 18 years and over (Meston et al., 2020). It assesses the reasons a person has engaged in sex, capturing how frequently each of 14 distinct motivations has led them to have sexual intercourse across their past sexual experiences. For respondents who have not previously had sex, the measure instead assesses the likelihood that each motivation would lead them to have sex.
5 minutes
Ages 18+
Formulation
Administer Now

context_sections.title: YSEX-SF Overview
context_sections.text:
People have sex for far more varied reasons than the familiar ones of pleasure, procreation, and love. The research programme behind the instrument identified 237 distinct reasons (Meston & Buss, 2007). Which of these motivations drive a person’s sexual behaviour carries meaningful information about their sexual desire, relationships, and wellbeing, and making those motivations explicit gives clinicians a structured way to understand what underlies a client’s sexual behaviour.
YSEX-SF Example Item

context_sections.title: YSEX-SF Subscales
context_sections.text:
The 14 subscales span physical, emotional, goal-oriented, and insecurity-related motivations for sex. Each is measured by two items.
Stress Reduction : sex used to release frustration, anxiety, or stress.
Pleasure : sex motivated by physical enjoyment and desire.
Physical Desirability : sex motivated by attraction to the other person’s appearance.
Experience Seeking : sex pursued for novelty, adventure, or excitement.
Resources : sex exchanged for tangible gain such as money or favours.
Reproduction : sex motivated by the desire to conceive.
Social Status : sex used to enhance reputation or standing.
Revenge : sex used to retaliate against a partner or get even with someone.
Practical : sex pursued for practical physical or emotional benefits.
Love and Commitment : sex used to express love and feel connected.
Expression : sex used to mark special occasions or transitions.
Self-Esteem Boost : sex used to feel better about oneself.
Duty/Pressure : sex engaged in out of obligation or in response to pressure.
Mate Guarding : sex used to keep a partner from straying.

context_sections.title: Clinical Applications of the YSEX-SF
context_sections.text:
The YSEX-SF was originally developed for research on sexual motivation and remains suited to that purpose. On NovoPsych it is applied clinically, chiefly to support formulation and feedback, rather than screening, diagnosis, or progress monitoring.
The measure can be used in sex therapy, relationship counselling, and general clinical practice wherever a client’s sexual behaviour, desire, or satisfaction is a focus of treatment. Its primary contribution is to formulation: the 14-subscale profile answers the question of what is driving a client’s sexual behaviour. A profile dominated by Duty/Pressure and Mate Guarding motivations tells a fundamentally different clinical story from one dominated by Pleasure and Love and Commitment motivations. The pattern of motivations across a profile can also clarify presentations involving mismatched desire, sexual dissatisfaction, or relationship insecurity.
The YSEX-SF supports psychoeducation and feedback conversations. The research behind the instrument documented a far wider range of sexual motivations than is typically assumed, and reviewing the profile collaboratively as part of treatment can normalise a client’s experience and open conversations that might not otherwise arise.
The measure provides a snapshot of the respondent’s motivational history rather than a measure of change over time. It functions closer to a structured screening of motivations than to an outcome measure, and is best used for formulation and feedback at a given point in care.

context_sections.title: YSEX-SF Scoring
context_sections.text:
All 28 items have response options ranging from 1 (None of my sexual experiences) to 5 (All of my sexual experiences). Each of the 14 subscales is scored by summing its two items, giving subscale scores from 2 to 10. Higher scores indicate that a greater proportion of the respondent’s sexual experiences have been motivated by that reason.
No total score is computed, and the measure has no norms, percentiles, or clinical cut-offs. The clinical output is the 14-subscale profile. For respondents who have not had sex, the instructions direct them to rate the likelihood that each reason would lead them to have sex, and their profile is read as anticipated rather than experienced motivation.
Subscale | Items | What it assesses
Stress Reduction | 1, 15 | Sex used to release frustration, anxiety, or stress. Higher scores may indicate that sex serves an emotion-regulation function.
Pleasure | 2, 16 | Sex motivated by physical enjoyment and desire. Typically among the most frequently endorsed motivations.
Physical Desirability | 3, 17 | Sex motivated by attraction to the other person’s appearance. The items refer to the person rather than a partner, reflecting that the measure covers casual and non-partnered sex.
Experience Seeking | 4, 18 | Sex pursued for novelty, adventure, or excitement.
Resources | 5, 19 | Sex exchanged for tangible gain such as money or favours. Elevated scores indicate that exchange-based motivations feature in the respondent’s experiences.
Reproduction | 6, 20 | Sex motivated by the desire to conceive. Scores are strongly context-dependent and interpreted in light of life stage and relationship circumstances.
Social Status | 7, 21 | Sex used to enhance reputation or standing.
Revenge | 8, 22 | Sex used to retaliate against a partner or get even with someone. Elevated scores may indicate unresolved relational conflict.
Practical | 9, 23 | Sex pursued for practical benefits. The two items span distinct content, one physical and one emotional, so reviewing them individually shows which is driving the score.
Love and Commitment | 10, 24 | Sex used to express love and feel connected. Low scores in a partnered respondent may be clinically informative about the relational function of sex.
Expression | 11, 25 | Sex used to mark special occasions or transitions, such as welcomes, farewells, and celebrations.
Self-Esteem Boost | 12, 26 | Sex used to feel better about oneself. Elevated scores may indicate that sexual activity is serving a self-worth regulation function.
Duty/Pressure | 13, 27 | Sex engaged in out of obligation or in response to pressure. Elevated scores can reflect experiences of sexual coercion.
Mate Guarding | 14, 28 | Sex used to keep a partner from straying. Elevated scores may indicate relationship insecurity or fear of abandonment.

context_sections.title: YSEX-SF Frequency Descriptors
context_sections.text:
Each subscale score is accompanied by a frequency descriptor taken directly from the measure’s own response options. Because each subscale consists of two items scored from 1 (None of my sexual experiences) to 5 (All of my sexual experiences), the summed subscale score can be translated back into the corresponding response scale to aid interpretation. These descriptors are not part of the original scoring system, and provide a plain-language summary of how frequently each motivation has contributed to the respondent’s sexual experiences.
Subscale score | Frequency descriptor
2 | None of my sexual experiences
3 to 4 | A few of my sexual experiences
5 to 6 | Some of my sexual experiences
7 to 8 | Many of my sexual experiences
9 to 10 | All of my sexual experiences
These descriptors are frequency labels rather than severity ratings or indicators of clinical significance. The clinical relevance of a given descriptor depends on the motivation being assessed and the respondent’s circumstances. A descriptor of Many of my sexual experiences may be expected for motivations such as Pleasure or Love and Commitment, whereas the same descriptor for Duty/Pressure may warrant further clinical exploration regarding possible coercion or unwanted sexual experiences.

context_sections.title: Interpreting the YSEX-SF Profile
context_sections.text:
The profile is interpreted relatively. The most clinically informative feature is which motivations are most and least frequent for the respondent, rather than the value of any single subscale in isolation. Considered together, the 14 subscale scores describe the overall shape of the respondent’s motivational profile.
Conceptually related subscales are often more informative in combination than any subscale considered alone. Representative examples include:
Frequent Duty/Pressure alongside frequent Mate Guarding may indicate that sex is functioning to preserve a relationship in which the person feels insecure, directing attention toward relational safety and communication.
Frequent Stress Reduction alongside frequent Self-Esteem Boost may indicate that sex is serving an emotion-regulation or self-worth function.
Frequent Pleasure, Love and Commitment, and Expression together describe sexual activity that is intrinsically and relationally motivated.
Infrequent Pleasure or Love and Commitment in a partnered respondent presenting with sexual dissatisfaction may itself be the clinically salient finding.

context_sections.title: Elevated Duty/Pressure
context_sections.text:
The Duty/Pressure items (I was pressured into doing it and I felt obligated to) can reflect experiences of sexual coercion. Where either item is endorsed above None of my sexual experiences, the report displays a note for the clinician showing both item responses, and adds a Duty/Pressure tag to the results dashboard. Clinicians are encouraged to review the individual item responses directly and follow up carefully to clarify the nature and context of these experiences.
Duty/Pressure is deliberately the only subscale carrying an automated clinician note. Elevations on Resources or Revenge can also carry clinical weight, but their meaning is more context-dependent, and they are left to the profile text and clinician review so the single high-stakes flag is not diluted.

context_sections.title: YSEX-SF Graphs
context_sections.text:
The report presents a horizontal bar chart of the 14 subscale scores, one bar per subscale, in a fixed order on an axis from 2 to 10. Five shaded vertical bands behind the bars mark the frequency-descriptor regions (None, A few, Some, Many, and All), deepening in shade from left to right, so each bar’s length can be read as its frequency descriptor and the overall shape of the profile is visible at a glance.

The chart shows the profile for the current administration. Repeat administrations regenerate the single-administration profile. No longitudinal score-tracking graphs are produced, consistent with the measure’s snapshot design.

context_sections.title: How could understanding someone's reasons for having sex be helpful in therapy?
context_sections.text: Sexual difficulties can sometimes be better understood once the motivations behind sexual behaviour are considered. Two clients with identical presentations, for example low desire, can have very different profiles: one may have sex mainly out of obligation and relationship insecurity, while the other’s profile centres on pleasure and connection that has recently declined. The YSEX-SF makes these patterns more explicit, helping the clinician and client build a shared formulation of what role sex plays in the client’s life and identify areas that may warrant further exploration.

context_sections.title: Is there a right or wrong reason to have sex?
context_sections.text:
No. The research behind the YSEX-SF identified over two hundred distinct reasons people have sex, spanning pleasure, love, curiosity, comfort, celebration, and many others, and most people endorse a mix. The measure describes how frequently each motivation has featured in the respondent’s experiences without judging any of them as necessarily positive or negative.
Some patterns may still warrant further clinical exploration. Sex motivated primarily by distress reduction or self-esteem enhancement may suggest an opportunity to explore broader coping strategies or emotional functioning.

context_sections.title: What does it mean if Duty/Pressure is among a client's most endorsed reasons?
context_sections.text: Frequent sex out of obligation or pressure can range from consensual but unwanted sex within a relationship through to experiences of sexual coercion. The NovoPsych report flags elevated Duty/Pressure scores for the clinician, and follow-up may be warranted: clarifying who or what the pressure comes from, whether it is current or historical, and how the client feels about these experiences. Depending on what emerges, treatment might focus on relational communication and consent, assertiveness, or processing past experiences.

context_sections.title: How does the YSEX-SF relate to the original YSEX? instrument?
context_sections.text: The original YSEX? contains over 140 items and was developed as a comprehensive research taxonomy of sexual motivation. The YSEX-SF was created by the same authors, who selected or wrote the two most representative items for each motivational domain, reducing completion time substantially while retaining the structure of the original. Scores on the short form correlate strongly with their long-form counterparts. The short form also introduced one new subscale, Reproduction, and renamed the Utilitarian subscale to Practical.

context_sections.title: Can someone complete the YSEX-SF if they have not had sex?
context_sections.text: Yes. The instructions ask respondents who have not had sex to rate how likely each reason would be to lead them to have sex. Their profile reflects anticipated rather than experienced motivation, which can still be clinically useful, for example in work with clients who are anxious about sexual relationships or exploring their readiness for them.

context_sections.title: Should clinicians focus on the highest-scoring subscale?
context_sections.text: Not necessarily. The pattern across subscales is often more informative than any single score. Most people report a combination of motivations rather than a single dominant reason, and results are best interpreted alongside the client’s history, presenting concerns, and broader clinical assessment.

Scoring and Interpretation Information
              Each of the 14 subscales is scored by summing its two items (response options 1 'None of my
              sexual experiences' to 5 'All of my sexual experiences'), giving subscale scores from 2 to 10.

              been motivated by that reason. No total score is computed and no norms, percentiles, or clinical
              cut-offs exist; the clinical output is the 14-subscale profile.

              Each subscale score is accompanied by a frequency descriptor derived from the response

sections.title: Why Have Sex? Questionnaire Short Form (YSEX-SF)
sections.text:
The Why Have Sex? Questionnaire Short Form (YSEX-SF) is a 28-item self-report measure of sexual motivation for adults aged 18 years and over (Meston et al., 2020). It assesses the reasons a person has engaged in sex, capturing how frequently each of 14 distinct motivations has led them to have sexual intercourse across their past sexual experiences. For respondents who have not previously had sex, the measure instead assesses the likelihood that each motivation would lead them to have sex.
5 minutes
Ages 18+
Formulation
Administer Now

sections.title: YSEX-SF Overview
sections.text:
People have sex for far more varied reasons than the familiar ones of pleasure, procreation, and love. The research programme behind the instrument identified 237 distinct reasons (Meston & Buss, 2007). Which of these motivations drive a person’s sexual behaviour carries meaningful information about their sexual desire, relationships, and wellbeing, and making those motivations explicit gives clinicians a structured way to understand what underlies a client’s sexual behaviour.
YSEX-SF Example Item

sections.title: YSEX-SF Subscales
sections.text:
The 14 subscales span physical, emotional, goal-oriented, and insecurity-related motivations for sex. Each is measured by two items.
Stress Reduction : sex used to release frustration, anxiety, or stress.
Pleasure : sex motivated by physical enjoyment and desire.
Physical Desirability : sex motivated by attraction to the other person’s appearance.
Experience Seeking : sex pursued for novelty, adventure, or excitement.
Resources : sex exchanged for tangible gain such as money or favours.
Reproduction : sex motivated by the desire to conceive.
Social Status : sex used to enhance reputation or standing.
Revenge : sex used to retaliate against a partner or get even with someone.
Practical : sex pursued for practical physical or emotional benefits.
Love and Commitment : sex used to express love and feel connected.
Expression : sex used to mark special occasions or transitions.
Self-Esteem Boost : sex used to feel better about oneself.
Duty/Pressure : sex engaged in out of obligation or in response to pressure.
Mate Guarding : sex used to keep a partner from straying.

sections.title: Clinical Applications of the YSEX-SF
sections.text:
The YSEX-SF was originally developed for research on sexual motivation and remains suited to that purpose. On NovoPsych it is applied clinically, chiefly to support formulation and feedback, rather than screening, diagnosis, or progress monitoring.
The measure can be used in sex therapy, relationship counselling, and general clinical practice wherever a client’s sexual behaviour, desire, or satisfaction is a focus of treatment. Its primary contribution is to formulation: the 14-subscale profile answers the question of what is driving a client’s sexual behaviour. A profile dominated by Duty/Pressure and Mate Guarding motivations tells a fundamentally different clinical story from one dominated by Pleasure and Love and Commitment motivations. The pattern of motivations across a profile can also clarify presentations involving mismatched desire, sexual dissatisfaction, or relationship insecurity.
The YSEX-SF supports psychoeducation and feedback conversations. The research behind the instrument documented a far wider range of sexual motivations than is typically assumed, and reviewing the profile collaboratively as part of treatment can normalise a client’s experience and open conversations that might not otherwise arise.
The measure provides a snapshot of the respondent’s motivational history rather than a measure of change over time. It functions closer to a structured screening of motivations than to an outcome measure, and is best used for formulation and feedback at a given point in care.

sections.title: YSEX-SF Scoring
sections.text:
All 28 items have response options ranging from 1 (None of my sexual experiences) to 5 (All of my sexual experiences). Each of the 14 subscales is scored by summing its two items, giving subscale scores from 2 to 10. Higher scores indicate that a greater proportion of the respondent’s sexual experiences have been motivated by that reason.
No total score is computed, and the measure has no norms, percentiles, or clinical cut-offs. The clinical output is the 14-subscale profile. For respondents who have not had sex, the instructions direct them to rate the likelihood that each reason would lead them to have sex, and their profile is read as anticipated rather than experienced motivation.
Subscale | Items | What it assesses
Stress Reduction | 1, 15 | Sex used to release frustration, anxiety, or stress. Higher scores may indicate that sex serves an emotion-regulation function.
Pleasure | 2, 16 | Sex motivated by physical enjoyment and desire. Typically among the most frequently endorsed motivations.
Physical Desirability | 3, 17 | Sex motivated by attraction to the other person’s appearance. The items refer to the person rather than a partner, reflecting that the measure covers casual and non-partnered sex.
Experience Seeking | 4, 18 | Sex pursued for novelty, adventure, or excitement.
Resources | 5, 19 | Sex exchanged for tangible gain such as money or favours. Elevated scores indicate that exchange-based motivations feature in the respondent’s experiences.
Reproduction | 6, 20 | Sex motivated by the desire to conceive. Scores are strongly context-dependent and interpreted in light of life stage and relationship circumstances.
Social Status | 7, 21 | Sex used to enhance reputation or standing.
Revenge | 8, 22 | Sex used to retaliate against a partner or get even with someone. Elevated scores may indicate unresolved relational conflict.
Practical | 9, 23 | Sex pursued for practical benefits. The two items span distinct content, one physical and one emotional, so reviewing them individually shows which is driving the score.
Love and Commitment | 10, 24 | Sex used to express love and feel connected. Low scores in a partnered respondent may be clinically informative about the relational function of sex.
Expression | 11, 25 | Sex used to mark special occasions or transitions, such as welcomes, farewells, and celebrations.
Self-Esteem Boost | 12, 26 | Sex used to feel better about oneself. Elevated scores may indicate that sexual activity is serving a self-worth regulation function.
Duty/Pressure | 13, 27 | Sex engaged in out of obligation or in response to pressure. Elevated scores can reflect experiences of sexual coercion.
Mate Guarding | 14, 28 | Sex used to keep a partner from straying. Elevated scores may indicate relationship insecurity or fear of abandonment.

sections.title: YSEX-SF Frequency Descriptors
sections.text:
Each subscale score is accompanied by a frequency descriptor taken directly from the measure’s own response options. Because each subscale consists of two items scored from 1 (None of my sexual experiences) to 5 (All of my sexual experiences), the summed subscale score can be translated back into the corresponding response scale to aid interpretation. These descriptors are not part of the original scoring system, and provide a plain-language summary of how frequently each motivation has contributed to the respondent’s sexual experiences.
Subscale score | Frequency descriptor
2 | None of my sexual experiences
3 to 4 | A few of my sexual experiences
5 to 6 | Some of my sexual experiences
7 to 8 | Many of my sexual experiences
9 to 10 | All of my sexual experiences
These descriptors are frequency labels rather than severity ratings or indicators of clinical significance. The clinical relevance of a given descriptor depends on the motivation being assessed and the respondent’s circumstances. A descriptor of Many of my sexual experiences may be expected for motivations such as Pleasure or Love and Commitment, whereas the same descriptor for Duty/Pressure may warrant further clinical exploration regarding possible coercion or unwanted sexual experiences.

sections.title: Interpreting the YSEX-SF Profile
sections.text:
The profile is interpreted relatively. The most clinically informative feature is which motivations are most and least frequent for the respondent, rather than the value of any single subscale in isolation. Considered together, the 14 subscale scores describe the overall shape of the respondent’s motivational profile.
Conceptually related subscales are often more informative in combination than any subscale considered alone. Representative examples include:
Frequent Duty/Pressure alongside frequent Mate Guarding may indicate that sex is functioning to preserve a relationship in which the person feels insecure, directing attention toward relational safety and communication.
Frequent Stress Reduction alongside frequent Self-Esteem Boost may indicate that sex is serving an emotion-regulation or self-worth function.
Frequent Pleasure, Love and Commitment, and Expression together describe sexual activity that is intrinsically and relationally motivated.
Infrequent Pleasure or Love and Commitment in a partnered respondent presenting with sexual dissatisfaction may itself be the clinically salient finding.

sections.title: Elevated Duty/Pressure
sections.text:
The Duty/Pressure items (I was pressured into doing it and I felt obligated to) can reflect experiences of sexual coercion. Where either item is endorsed above None of my sexual experiences, the report displays a note for the clinician showing both item responses, and adds a Duty/Pressure tag to the results dashboard. Clinicians are encouraged to review the individual item responses directly and follow up carefully to clarify the nature and context of these experiences.
Duty/Pressure is deliberately the only subscale carrying an automated clinician note. Elevations on Resources or Revenge can also carry clinical weight, but their meaning is more context-dependent, and they are left to the profile text and clinician review so the single high-stakes flag is not diluted.

sections.title: YSEX-SF Graphs
sections.text:
The report presents a horizontal bar chart of the 14 subscale scores, one bar per subscale, in a fixed order on an axis from 2 to 10. Five shaded vertical bands behind the bars mark the frequency-descriptor regions (None, A few, Some, Many, and All), deepening in shade from left to right, so each bar’s length can be read as its frequency descriptor and the overall shape of the profile is visible at a glance.

The chart shows the profile for the current administration. Repeat administrations regenerate the single-administration profile. No longitudinal score-tracking graphs are produced, consistent with the measure’s snapshot design.

sections.title: Development of the YSEX-SF
sections.text:
The original taxonomy for the 142-item YSEX? was developed in two stages (Meston & Buss, 2007). First, 444 participants nominated reasons for having sex, producing 237 distinct reasons. These were administered to 1,549 undergraduate students, and factor analyses yielded a hierarchical structure of four broad factors (Physical, Goal Attainment, Emotional, and Insecurity reasons) comprising 13 subfactors. The long-form instrument demonstrated strong internal consistency, with alphas exceeding .85 for each factor score.
The YSEX-SF was developed by Meston and colleagues from this same dataset (Meston et al., 2020, Study 1). The two most representative items for each subscale were selected using the original factor loadings combined with structured consensus judgements of conceptual fit. Where the original items were too specific to represent a subscale in two items, broader composite items were written. Two structural changes were made: the items concerning conception were separated from the Resources subscale into a new Reproduction subscale, and the Utilitarian subscale was renamed Practical. The result is a 28-item instrument with 14 subscales of two items each, an item reduction of just over 80 percent, that maintains the original instrument’s sound psychometric properties.
No standalone official copy of the YSEX-SF exists. The instrument’s first author has confirmed that the short form is administered by presenting the 28 retained items with the full-length YSEX? instructions and response options (C. M. Meston, personal communication, July 22, 2026). This is how NovoPsych presents it.

sections.title: YSEX-SF Reliability
sections.text:
Internal consistency was assessed in a validation sample of 223 United States adults recruited online (ages 19 to 76, median 33; Meston et al., 2020, Study 2). The two-item subscale alphas ranged from .42 to .93, with an average of .74. Reliability was strongest for Reproduction (α = .93), Mate Guarding (α = .82), Resources (α = .81), Stress Reduction (α = .80), and Physical Desirability (α = .80), and acceptable for most remaining subscales, including Love and Commitment (α = .78), Social Status (α = .76), Experience Seeking (α = .75), Duty/Pressure (α = .75), Self-Esteem Boost (α = .74), and Revenge (α = .70). Pleasure (α = .68) and Expression (α = .62) showed more modest internal consistency, and Practical was the weakest subscale (α = .42), reflecting its two items spanning distinct physical and emotional benefits.
Because Cronbach’s alpha rises with the number of items, two-item subscales tend to produce lower coefficients than longer scales. These values should be read with the short scale length in mind rather than as evidence of weak items.

sections.title: YSEX-SF Factor Structure
sections.text:
A confirmatory factor analysis in the validation sample (N = 218) supported the 14-factor structure, with acceptable model fit (CFI = 0.91, TLI = 0.86, RMSEA = 0.070, 90% CI [0.061, 0.078]) and standardised item loadings ranging from .52 to .92, excluding the variance-constrained Reproduction item whose corrected loading is reported as 1.00. The initial solution produced a negative residual variance (a Heywood case) for one Reproduction item (I wanted to have a child), resolved by constraining that item’s residual variance to be above zero with no meaningful loss of fit.
The 14 factors are modelled as correlated dimensions, consistent with the observation that reasons for having sex are not mutually exclusive. A person can have sex both out of obligation and to feel connected to their partner.

sections.title: YSEX-SF Validity
sections.text:
Cross-form validity between the YSEX-SF and the full-length YSEX? was generally strong (Meston et al., 2020, Study 2). Twelve of the 14 subscales correlated between r = .61 and r = .85 with their long-form counterparts. The Practical subscale correlated moderately with the long-form Utilitarian subscale (r = .43), reflecting the substantial condensing of that subscale’s content, and the new Reproduction subscale correlated moderately with the long-form Resources subscale from which its items were drawn (r = .39), consistent with its deliberate isolation as a distinct construct.
Construct validity was supported by theoretically coherent associations with personality and sexual-strategy measures. Higher scores on all three Dark Triad traits (Machiavellianism, narcissism, and psychopathy) were associated with more frequent Social Status, Revenge, and Mate Guarding motivations in both men and women. Love and Commitment showed no association with any Dark Triad trait in either gender, supporting the discriminant validity of the profile. Sociosexual orientation (openness to uncommitted sex) was associated with more frequent Revenge motivations in both genders, and with less frequent Love and Commitment motivation in women.

sections.title: YSEX-SF Gender Comparisons
sections.text: Gender differences on the YSEX-SF were small. Men scored higher than women on the three largest differences in motivation: Physical Desirability (d = 0.37), Social Status (d = 0.35), and Experience Seeking (d = 0.33). The largest difference on which women scored higher was Love and Commitment (d = 0.27). None of these differences remained statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons (Meston et al., 2020). Scores are therefore interpreted without reference to gender.

sections.title: YSEX-SF Norms
sections.text: NovoPsych does not calculate YSEX-SF percentiles. The only available normative data come from the validation sample of 223 United States adults recruited online, reported separately by gender, with pronounced floor effects on several subscales because most respondents endorse None of my sexual experiences for motivations such as Resources, Revenge, and Reproduction. Percentiles derived from that sample would imply a reference comparison and a degree of precision the data do not support. The measure also has no clinical cut-offs anywhere in the literature. Interpretation therefore rests on the frequency descriptors and the shape of the profile.

sections.title: How could understanding someone's reasons for having sex be helpful in therapy?
sections.text: Sexual difficulties can sometimes be better understood once the motivations behind sexual behaviour are considered. Two clients with identical presentations, for example low desire, can have very different profiles: one may have sex mainly out of obligation and relationship insecurity, while the other’s profile centres on pleasure and connection that has recently declined. The YSEX-SF makes these patterns more explicit, helping the clinician and client build a shared formulation of what role sex plays in the client’s life and identify areas that may warrant further exploration.

sections.title: Is there a right or wrong reason to have sex?
sections.text:
No. The research behind the YSEX-SF identified over two hundred distinct reasons people have sex, spanning pleasure, love, curiosity, comfort, celebration, and many others, and most people endorse a mix. The measure describes how frequently each motivation has featured in the respondent’s experiences without judging any of them as necessarily positive or negative.
Some patterns may still warrant further clinical exploration. Sex motivated primarily by distress reduction or self-esteem enhancement may suggest an opportunity to explore broader coping strategies or emotional functioning.

sections.title: What does it mean if Duty/Pressure is among a client's most endorsed reasons?
sections.text: Frequent sex out of obligation or pressure can range from consensual but unwanted sex within a relationship through to experiences of sexual coercion. The NovoPsych report flags elevated Duty/Pressure scores for the clinician, and follow-up may be warranted: clarifying who or what the pressure comes from, whether it is current or historical, and how the client feels about these experiences. Depending on what emerges, treatment might focus on relational communication and consent, assertiveness, or processing past experiences.

sections.title: How does the YSEX-SF relate to the original YSEX? instrument?
sections.text: The original YSEX? contains over 140 items and was developed as a comprehensive research taxonomy of sexual motivation. The YSEX-SF was created by the same authors, who selected or wrote the two most representative items for each motivational domain, reducing completion time substantially while retaining the structure of the original. Scores on the short form correlate strongly with their long-form counterparts. The short form also introduced one new subscale, Reproduction, and renamed the Utilitarian subscale to Practical.

sections.title: Can someone complete the YSEX-SF if they have not had sex?
sections.text: Yes. The instructions ask respondents who have not had sex to rate how likely each reason would be to lead them to have sex. Their profile reflects anticipated rather than experienced motivation, which can still be clinically useful, for example in work with clients who are anxious about sexual relationships or exploring their readiness for them.

sections.title: Should clinicians focus on the highest-scoring subscale?
sections.text: Not necessarily. The pattern across subscales is often more informative than any single score. Most people report a combination of motivations rather than a single dominant reason, and results are best interpreted alongside the client’s history, presenting concerns, and broader clinical assessment.

source_rule_excerpts: The BAM is a monitoring instrument, not a screener or diagnostic test, and it does not have an established cut-off score or general-population norms. Reporting raw domain scores and their change over time reflects how the measure is best used: as a way to track a specific client’s progress against their own earlier scores, rather than to rank them against a reference group. A consistent downward movement in a client’s Substance Use or Risk Factors score over several weeks is clinically informative in its own right, without needing a percentile.

There are no norms, cut-scores, or percentile ranks for the BAM domain scores, and the measure does not produce a total score. Results are compared against the same client’s earlier administrations rather than against a reference population. There is no threshold at which a domain score becomes “high” or “clinically significant.”

A reduction in the Substance Use or Risk Factors domain, or an increase in the Protective Factors domain, reflects movement in the favourable direction. Movement on Protective Factors should be read with particular caution: the internal consistency of that domain is very low (Cronbach’s alpha .32 and .22; Hallinan et al., 2021), so a change in the total should always be checked against which of its six items actually moved. Change is reported as a raw point difference. No threshold defines how large a change must be before it counts as meaningful. Change is therefore read directionally and in the context of the client’s own trajectory.

Background gradient. All plots carry a background gradient whose colour deepens as more of the construct is present: red as Substance Use and Risk Factors scores rise, green as Protective Factors scores rise. On the trajectory plots the gradient is a wash behind the line; on the single-administration plots it is a strip along the base of each chart. Only the upper portion of each scale is shaded, and the shading fades out gradually rather than beginning at a fixed point. The lower end is left unshaded deliberately: a low Substance Use or Risk Factors score reflects the absence of a reported problem rather than a positive finding. The shading is a visual guide only. The BAM has no validated cut scores, norms, or severity bands, so no score should be read as having crossed a threshold on the basis of where it falls within the gradient.

source_guidance.title: BAM Scoring
source_guidance.text:
Item-level scoring. Each BAM item is scored from 0 to 30. Items asking for a number of days or nights over the past month (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7a to 7g, 10, 11, 13, and 16) are scored as the actual number reported. Items with five rated response options (1, 8, 9, 12, 15, and 17) are scored 0, 8, 15, 22, or 30. Item 14, which asks whether the respondent has adequate legal income, is scored No = 0 and Yes = 30.
Contingent items. Two conditional blocks are displayed only if the respondent reported any use on the preceding item, covering eight items in total. If the respondent reports no alcohol use in the past 30 days (i.e., item 4 = 0 days), the heavy-drinking item (item 5) is skipped; if they report no drug use (i.e., item 6 = 0 days), the seven specific-drug items (7a to 7g) are skipped. Skipped items are scored zero, so the domain totals remain on the same scale for every client. Note that a skipped item still appears in the Client Responses table as “Not Completed”: item 5 whenever item 4 is zero, and items 7a to 7g whenever item 6 is zero. A “Not Completed” entry against one of these items means the question was not asked because the preceding answer made it redundant, not that data are missing, and the Substance Use total is complete.

source_guidance.title: BAM Domain Score Interpretation
source_guidance.text:
The BAM is interpreted using raw domain scores and interpretation is directional. On the Substance Use and Risk Factor domains, higher scores indicate more substance use and more risk-related circumstances. On the Protective Factors domain, higher scores indicate more recovery support. A single administration gives a snapshot of where the client currently sits across the three domains; the greatest clinical value comes from comparing scores across administrations to see what is improving and what is not.
Because each BAM item reflects a distinct and concrete behaviour or state, reviewing individual item responses is often as informative as the domain totals. Items carry richer implications for treatment planning than the composite scores. A high number of days of drug use, a rise in risky situations, or a fall in self-help attendance each points to a specific and actionable focus for the next stage of treatment. Two clients with the same Risk score may present entirely differently: one with physical health, sleep and mood difficulties, the other with craving, risky situations and interpersonal conflict; so the total domain score alone cannot guide the plan.
The items the report surfaces in its interpretive text are selected and ordered by score on the shared 0 to 30 metric, not by clinical importance, so that list is a starting point for review rather than a priority order. The full set of responses is set out at the end of the report, grouped by domain and numbered as they appear on the questionnaire (1 to 17, with 7a to 7g), so each answer can be reviewed directly alongside the domain totals.

Results are compared against the same client’s earlier administrations rather than against a reference population. There is no threshold at which a domain score becomes “high” or “clinically significant.”

source_guidance.title: BAM Change Score Interpretation
source_guidance.text:
The BAM is designed for repeated administration as part of measurement-based care (MBC), and change across administrations is the primary interpretive output.
On a repeat administration the report describes change against two reference points: the most recent prior administration, and the client’s initial administration. Reporting both separates a recent shift from the overall trajectory, which can move in opposite directions. On a second administration the two reference points are the same, so only one comparison is given.
A reduction in the Substance Use or Risk Factors domain, or an increase in the Protective Factors domain, reflects movement in the favourable direction. Movement on Protective Factors should be read with particular caution: the internal consistency of that domain is very low (Cronbach’s alpha .32 and .22; Hallinan et al., 2021), so a change in the total should always be checked against which of its six items actually moved. Change is reported as a raw point difference. No threshold defines how large a change must be before it counts as meaningful. Change is therefore read directionally and in the context of the client’s own trajectory.
The evidence base indicates that BAM scores move meaningfully during treatment, with the heavy alcohol use, drug use, craving, mood, and self-help items showing the greatest responsiveness (Blanchard et al., 2023).

source_guidance.title: BAM Substance Use Domain Score Graph Over Time
source_guidance.text: Background gradient. All plots carry a background gradient whose colour deepens as more of the construct is present: red as Substance Use and Risk Factors scores rise, green as Protective Factors scores rise. On the trajectory plots the gradient is a wash behind the line; on the single-administration plots it is a strip along the base of each chart. Only the upper portion of each scale is shaded, and the shading fades out gradually rather than beginning at a fixed point. The lower end is left unshaded deliberately: a low Substance Use or Risk Factors score reflects the absence of a reported problem rather than a positive finding. The shading is a visual guide only. The BAM has no validated cut scores, norms, or severity bands, so no score should be read as having crossed a threshold on the basis of where it falls within the gradient.

source_guidance.title: Why does the BAM report raw scores rather than percentiles or a cut-off?
source_guidance.text: The BAM is a monitoring instrument, not a screener or diagnostic test, and it does not have an established cut-off score or general-population norms. Reporting raw domain scores and their change over time reflects how the measure is best used: as a way to track a specific client’s progress against their own earlier scores, rather than to rank them against a reference group. A consistent downward movement in a client’s Substance Use or Risk Factors score over several weeks is clinically informative in its own right, without needing a percentile.

source_guidance.title: Why might a client's scores get worse during treatment?
source_guidance.text: An increase in the Substance Use or Risk Factors score, or a fall in the Protective Factors score, does not necessarily mean treatment is failing. Scores can rise as clients become more honest in their reporting as trust builds, or in response to a stressful period, a lapse, or a change in circumstances. Rather than reading a single upward movement as a setback, it is more useful to view the trajectory across several administrations and to use any deterioration as a prompt for discussion about what has changed for the client.
