sections.text:
The Mood and Feelings Questionnaire – Self Report (Short Version) (MFQ-Self) is a 13-item self-report measure developed to assess core depressive symptoms in children and adolescents aged 6 to 17 years over the past two weeks (Angold et al., 1995). It was created as an abbreviated version of the 33-item Mood and Feelings Questionnaire to provide a brief, psychometrically sound instrument suitable for clinical screening. The MFQ-Self has been recommended by the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) guidelines as a screening tool for childhood and adolescent depression (Middleton et al., 2005). In addition to the self-report version a parallel parent-report version is also available. Using both versions together can give a clearer picture of the youth’s symptoms at home and in daily life.
MFQ-Self Example Item

While the MFQ-Self is commonly referred to as the Short Mood and Feelings Questionnaire (SMFQ) in the literature, NovoPsych uses the abbreviated name, MFQ-Self, throughout this report. The MFQ-Self was designed based on DSM diagnostic classifications, with items selected according to their correlations with the full MFQ-Self total scores, factor loadings, and associations with clinical status and depression diagnosis (Angold et al., 1995). While there are no subscales, items assess a range of cognitive and affective components of depressive symptoms, including negative self-evaluation, low mood, and anhedonia, whilst also capturing symptoms of tiredness, restlessness, and poor concentration (Sharp et al., 2006; Thabrew et al., 2018; Turner et al., 2014).
Depression is a significant public health concern amongst young people, affecting up to one in five youth before reaching 18 years of age (Lewinsohn et al., 1993). Youth-onset depression is particularly concerning due to its association with poorer educational attainment, impaired interpersonal relationships, increased risk of recurrence in adulthood, and elevated rates of suicidality (Copeland et al., 2009; Hammen et al., 2008). The MFQ-Self addresses a critical need for efficient depression screening in clinical and research settings, as comprehensive diagnostic interviews are time-intensive and may not be feasible for large-scale screening programmes.
TheMFQ-Self can be used to aid clinicians in multiple ways within comprehensive mental health care, including initial screening to identify youth who require diagnostic evaluation and further assessment. It also serves as a valuable tool for tracking symptom changes during treatment, with research demonstrating sensitivity to therapeutic interventions (Thabrew et al., 2018). The MFQ-Self can also support treatment planning by providing a quantifiable baseline of symptom severity and by identifying specific symptom domains warranting clinical attention. For instance, elevated scores on items assessing concentration difficulties and tiredness may suggest the need for psychoeducation about sleep hygiene, whilst high scores on items related to negative self-evaluation may indicate that cognitive restructuring would be beneficial. Additionally, the MFQ-Self can identify depression in young people who may have difficulty verbally articulating their internal experiences, as the structured format and concrete response options make the assessment more accessible than open-ended clinical interviews for some youth.

sections.title: MFQ-Self Scoring & Interpretation
sections.text:
Each of the 13 MFQ-Self items are scored 0 (not true), 1 (sometimes), or 2 (true), reflecting the frequency of depressive symptoms experienced over the past 2 weeks. The sum of responses to all items produces a total score ranging from 0 to 26. Higher scores indicate greater severity of depressive symptoms.

Based on empirical research and established cut-off values, scores can be interpreted using three severity categories.
Minimal: 0-7: Total scores below 8 fall within the range typically observed in community samples and indicate minimal to no clinically significant depression.
Elevated: 8-11: Total scores of 8 to 11 indicate the presence of clinically significant depressive symptoms that sit at the 75th percentile compared to a community sample, and the 25th percentile of a clinical sample.
Severe: 12+: Total scores of 12 and above represent a higher severity category at approximately the 95th percentile in community samples and the 50th percentile in clinical samples. This severity category comes from a threshold identified by Thabrew et al. (2018) in adolescent samples (ranging 11-19 years old), optimally distinguished young people meeting diagnostic criteria for a depressive disorder from those with subthreshold symptoms.
The MFQ-Self can be used for monitoring symptom changes over time during treatment. Research examining meaningful score changes suggests a 2-point change in either direction represents a noticeable shift in symptom severity.
On first administration, a bar graph displaying the total raw score is presented.

A comparison graph is also displayed showing the client’s score relative to community data from Schlechter et al. (2023) and clinical data from Thabrew et al. (2018).

When the assessment is administered multiple times, a longitudinal line graph is generated to track changes in the total raw score over time.

sections.title: MFQ-Self Psychometrics
sections.text:
The MFQ-Self demonstrates strong construct validity through multiple lines of evidence. The scale shows robust convergent validity with other measures of depression and related constructs. The scale has been observed to be strongly correlated with the Children’s Depression Rating Scale-Revised (CDRS-R; r = .66 to .71) and the Reynolds Adolescent Depression Scale-2 (RADS-2; r = .83 to .85) across multiple time points (Thabrew et al., 2018). The scale also demonstrates moderate to strong correlations with theoretically related constructs, including anxiety (r = .57- .62) and quality of life (r = -.73–.77) (Thabrew et al., 2018). Research examining associations with external validators found significant correlations with psychotic symptoms (r = .16-.34), anxiety symptoms (r = .16-.72), life events (r = .10-.23), and self-rated health (r = .13-.40), supporting the scale’s ability to capture clinically meaningful variation in depressive symptomatology (Schlechter et al., 2023).
The MFQ-Self exhibits excellent internal consistency across diverse samples and age groups. Cronbach’s alpha coefficients consistently fall within the good to excellent range, including α = .88 to .89 in New Zealand help-seeking adolescents (Thabrew et al., 2018), α = .84 in a community sample of 11-13 year olds (Rhew et al., 2010), α = .92 in young adults aged 25 years (Eyre et al., 2021), and α = .80 to .91 in various samples aged 6 to 17 years (Angold et al., 1995).
The MFQ-Self has been extensively validated as a unidimensional measure. Confirmatory factor analyses consistently support a single-factor structure across development from early adolescence through emerging adulthood (Thabrew et al., 2018; Turner et al., 2014). Research examining measurement invariance found that the MFQ-Self displays strict factor invariance from ages 14 to 26 years, indicating that the scale measures the same underlying depression construct consistently across this developmental period (Schlechter et al., 2023). The scale also demonstrates measurement invariance across sex at most ages studied, supporting its use for making valid comparisons between males and females. The robust unidimensional structure provides strong justification for using sum scores in clinical contexts (Schlechter et al., 2023).
Criterion validity has been established through numerous studies examining the MFQ-Self’s ability to discriminate between depressed and non-depressed youth. Across samples aged 6 to 17 years, the scale demonstrates acceptable to good sensitivity ranging from .60 to .86, specificity from .61 to .87, and discrimination ability with area under the curve (AUC) values of .72 to .84 when compared against structured clinical interviews (Angold et al., 1995; Rhew et al., 2010; Thabrew et al., 2018). In a large community sample of 25-year-olds, the MFQ-Self achieved high accuracy for discriminating major depressive disorder cases from non-cases with an AUC of .92 (Eyre et al., 2021). The scale also demonstrates sensitivity to change following treatment, with strong correlations between MFQ-Self change scores and clinician-rated change in depression severity (r = .64) and comparable effect sizes to established depression measures (Thabrew et al., 2018).
Normative data for the MFQ-Self have been reported across multiple samples. The most comprehensive community normative data come from Schlechter et al. (2023), who examined the MFQ-Self in a large epidemiological sample (N = 6,019) from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children. At Wave 3 (mean age 13 years), the community sample demonstrated a mean total score of 4.92 (SD = 4.49). Thabrew et al. (2017) provided normative data from a clinical sample of New Zealand help-seeking adolescents (N = 186, mean age 15.6 years) with a mean total score of 12.1 (SD = 6.0). These samples provide valuable comparison groups for interpreting scores.
The establishment of cut-off scores for the MFQ-Self has received considerable attention in the literature. Angold et al. (1995), established a cut-off of 8 or above to indicate clinically significant depressive symptoms. More recently, Thabrew et al. (2017) conducted receiver operating characteristic analyses in their help-seeking adolescent sample, favouring sensitivity over specificity to ensure identification of youth requiring further assessment. They identified an optimal cut-off value of 12 or above, which yielded sensitivity of 84.2% and specificity of 68.2%, with an AUC of .86. This higher cut-off represents a score at the 94th percentile of community samples and provides a threshold for a higher category of symptom severity that can be used alongside the cut off specified by Angold et al. (1995). Other studies suggested varying cut-offs, such as a score of 4 (Rhew et al., 2010), however, this yielded poor specificity. For the purposes of aiding in clinical interpretation, both the original cut-off of 8 and the heightened cut-off of 12 provide useful anchoring points for understanding depression severity.
In consideration of the standard and heightened cut-offs, and with respect to the clinical and community normative data, severity category interpretation guidelines are provided here:
0-7: Total scores below 8 fall within the range typically observed in community samples and indicate minimal to no clinically significant depression.
8-11: Total scores of 8 to 11 indicate the presence of clinically significant depressive symptoms that sit at the 75th percentile compared to a community sample, and the 25th percentile of a clinical sample.
12+: Total scores of 12 and above represent a higher severity category at approximately the 95th percentile in community samples and the 50th percentile in clinical samples. This severity category comes from a threshold identified by Thabrew et al. (2018) in adolescent samples (ranging 11-19 years old), optimally distinguished young people meeting diagnostic criteria for a depressive disorder from those with subthreshold symptoms.
The 12+ category identified by Thabrew et al (2018) and presented here as an indicator of heightened severity, has only been validated in adolescents aged 11-19 years and so should be interpreted with caution when used with younger children aged 6-10 years.

Why screen for depression in children and adolescents?
Depression in young people often presents differently than in adults and can be easily overlooked. Adolescents may display irritability rather than sadness, whilst children might show behavioural problems or somatic complaints rather than verbalising low mood. Early identification is crucial because youth-onset depression is associated with significant long-term consequences, including poorer educational outcomes, difficulties in relationships, increased risk of depression recurrence in adulthood, and elevated rates of self-harm and suicidal behaviour. Many young people find it difficult to articulate their emotional experiences in clinical interviews, making structured screening tools like the MFQ-Self valuable for identifying those who might benefit from intervention. Regular screening in mental health settings, schools, and primary care can help catch emerging difficulties before they become entrenched, allowing for earlier intervention when treatment is often most effective.
Can the MFQ-Self be used with younger children aged 6-10 years?
The MFQ-Self is validated for use from age 6, however, clinicians should consider developmental factors when administering it to younger children. Children in this age range may have limited insight into their internal emotional states and may interpret items more concretely than intended. For instance, “I felt I was no good anymore” requires a level of abstract self-reflection that some younger children haven’t yet developed. In these cases, the parent-report version becomes particularly valuable, as caregivers can often better observe behavioural manifestations of depression in younger children, such as irritability, social withdrawal, or changes in play and activity levels.
Can the MFQ-Self be used to monitor treatment progress?
Yes, the MFQ-Self is well-suited to repeated use throughout treatment, with research suggesting that a 2-point change in either direction represents a noticeable shift in symptom severity. Clinicians can administer the measure at regular intervals to track treatment progress. The brief format is also beneficial in minimising assessment burden, making frequent administration feasible.
Can I use both the self-report and parent versions together?
Yes, and using both versions together can provide a more comprehensive picture of a young person’s symptoms. Children and adolescents may minimise their difficulties, particularly internalised symptoms like negative self-evaluation or feelings of worthlessness, whilst parents might not be fully aware of their child’s internal emotional experiences. Discrepancies between versions can be clinically meaningful, for instance, if a parent reports minimal symptoms but the young person scores in the elevated range, this might indicate the child is concealing their difficulties or that symptoms are more apparent in settings outside the home. Conversely, higher parent-reported scores might suggest observable behavioural changes that the young person hasn’t yet recognised themselves.

assessment.name: Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Child Self Report (ChOCI-R-S)
assessment.description: The Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) is a 38-item self-report measure of obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) symptoms (Uher et al., 2008) in children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. It is completed by the child or adolescent and measures both the obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviours they experience and the impairment these cause in daily life. There is also a parent-report version of the ChOCI ( ChOCI-R-P ) that can be completed by a parent or caregiver.

administration.instructions: Each of the following questions asks you about things or “habits” you feel you have to do although you may know that they do not make sense. Sometimes, you may try to stop from doing them but this might not be possible. You might feel worried or angry or frustrated until you have finished what you have to do. An example of a habit like this may be the need to wash your hands over and over again even though they are not really dirty, or the need to count up to a special number (e.g. 6 or 10) while you do certain things. Please answer each question by indicating how much you agree with the statement, or how much you think it is true of you. Please answer each item, without spending too much time on any one item. There are no right or wrong answers. Compulsions· symptoms

scoring.coverage: Implemented formulas have explicit item membership and numeric source evidence. Remaining expressions, diagnostic algorithms, percentiles, custom missing-answer policies and interpretation require review.
source_rule_excerpts: Total Symptoms (sum of Compulsion Symptoms and Obsession Symptoms; scores range from 0 to 40) Compulsion Symptoms (items 1 to 10; scores range from 0 to 20): sum of 10 items Obsession Symptoms (items 20 to 29; scores range from 0 to 20): sum of 10 items

Total Impairment (sum of Compulsion Impairment and Obsession Impairment; scores range from 0 to 48) Compulsion Impairment (items 14 to 19; scores range from 0 to 24): sum of 6 items Obsession Impairment (items 33 to 38; scores range from 0 to 24): sum of 6 items

Each raw score is presented with a percentile rank against an OCD-clinical reference sample. A percentile of 50 corresponds to the OCD-clinical reference average; a percentile of 80 indicates a score exceeding approximately 80% of young people with OCD in the reference group. Because the norms come from an OCD-diagnosed sample, a low percentile does not mean a young person does not have OCD, only that their symptoms or impairment are milder than most others with the condition.

On first administration, the report presents a results table followed by two construct sections (Symptoms and Impairment). Each section contains two horizontal raw-score charts. The first plots the construct’s total as a single bar with the client’s raw score on a 0–40 axis for Symptoms or 0–48 for Impairment. A clinical 25th-to-75th percentile reference rectangle and a dashed line at the clinical average show the score relative to the clinical reference sample of young people with OCD. The second plots the construct’s two subscales (Compulsion and Obsession bars on a 0–20 axis for Symptoms or 0–24 for Impairment, each with its own 25th-to-75th reference rectangle and clinical-average line). Beneath each bar, a coloured strip marks that scale’s descriptor bands (Low, Moderate and High for Symptoms; Minimal, Mild, Moderate, Severe and Extreme for Impairment, with Minimal shown in white).

Reference percentiles are derived from Uher and colleagues (2008): 285 consecutive referrals (244 to 278 with complete self-report data per subscale) to an OCD clinic between 2000 and 2006, all meeting ICD-10 criteria for OCD via structured clinical interview, with no significant sex differences (boys’ age M = 13.7, range 7 to 18; girls’ age M = 13.7, range 9 to 18). Reference parameters for the self-report subscales are: Compulsion Symptoms M = 9.5, SD = 4.3; Obsession Symptoms M = 8.0, SD = 5.1; Total Symptoms M = 17.6, SD = 7.8; Compulsion Impairment M = 15.0, SD = 4.5; Obsession Impairment M = 13.5, SD = 5.2; Total Impairment M = 28.5, SD = 8.7. Because this reference sample is clinical (not community), percentile interpretation is positional within an OCD-diagnosed reference group: a percentile of 50 reflects the average level for a young person diagnosed with OCD, not the general population. No community-sample reference data exists for the self-report ChOCI-R-S, and the original authors note that confirmation in primary care and population-based samples remains needed (Uher et al., 2008).

The descriptors are a descriptive guide, not diagnostic cut-offs, and do not replace clinical judgement. NovoPsych placed each subscale’s cut-offs at the same percentile as the matching Total cut-off, using each subscale’s own mean and SD from Uher et al. (2008), with each band starting at the next whole score. For symptoms, Moderate starts at about the 16th percentile and High at about the 84th. For impairment, Mild starts at about the 1st–2nd percentile, Moderate about the 16th, Severe about the 56th and Extreme about the 90th. The parent-report ChOCI-R-P has different raw-score cut-offs, because each form is converted through its own column of the equivalence table and its own norms, so the same raw score does not mean the same thing on the two forms.

source_guidance.title: Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) Scoring
source_guidance.text:
The Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory–Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) produces six raw scores by summing item responses. Higher scores indicate more obsessive-compulsive symptoms or greater associated functional impairment. The ChOCI-R-S measures both symptoms and impairment:
Total Symptoms (sum of Compulsion Symptoms and Obsession Symptoms; scores range from 0 to 40) Compulsion Symptoms (items 1 to 10; scores range from 0 to 20): sum of 10 items Obsession Symptoms (items 20 to 29; scores range from 0 to 20): sum of 10 items
Total Impairment (sum of Compulsion Impairment and Obsession Impairment; scores range from 0 to 48) Compulsion Impairment (items 14 to 19; scores range from 0 to 24): sum of 6 items Obsession Impairment (items 33 to 38; scores range from 0 to 24): sum of 6 items
Six open-text items (items 11 to 13 for habits and items 30 to 32 for thoughts) ask the young person to describe their three most upsetting habits (compulsions) and thoughts (obsessions), respectively. These items are not included in the scoring, but provide additional clinical information to inform assessment and treatment planning.

source_guidance.title: ChOCI-R-S Percentiles
source_guidance.text: Each raw score is presented with a percentile rank against an OCD-clinical reference sample. A percentile of 50 corresponds to the OCD-clinical reference average; a percentile of 80 indicates a score exceeding approximately 80% of young people with OCD in the reference group. Because the norms come from an OCD-diagnosed sample, a low percentile does not mean a young person does not have OCD, only that their symptoms or impairment are milder than most others with the condition.

source_guidance.title: Subscale interpretation of the ChOCI-R-S
source_guidance.text: Each ChOCI-R-S subscale assesses a different aspect of obsessive-compulsive symptoms or associated impairment. Higher scores on Compulsion Symptoms indicate that the young person reports more frequent or more severe compulsive behaviours, such as washing, checking, ordering, counting and reassurance-seeking. Higher scores on Obsession Symptoms indicate more frequent intrusive thoughts of harm, doubt, death, religious or blasphemous content, or aggressive or immoral content. Higher scores on Compulsion Impairment indicate greater functional disruption from compulsions, including time spent, interference with school and friends, distress when prevented from acting, difficulty resisting or controlling compulsions, and avoidance. Higher scores on Obsession Impairment indicate similar impacts associated with obsessive thoughts.

source_guidance.title: ChOCI-R-S Change Score Interpretation
source_guidance.text: When the ChOCI-R-S is administered on multiple occasions, change between administrations can be evaluated using a Reliable Change Index (RCI). A change of approximately 9.0 raw-score points or greater on Total Impairment, or 8.6 or greater on Total Symptoms, indicates a change that is unlikely to be attributable to measurement error alone.

source_guidance.title: ChOCI-R-S Change Score Interpretation
source_guidance.text: When the ChOCI-R-S is administered on multiple occasions, change between administrations is interpreted via a Reliable Change Index (RCI) computed with the Jacobson-Truax formula, using the Uher and colleagues (2008) self-report internal consistency reliability and standard deviation for each total. A change of approximately 9.0 raw-score points or greater on Total Impairment (alpha = .86, SD = 8.7), or 8.6 or greater on Total Symptoms (alpha = .84, SD = 7.8), exceeds measurement error at the 95% confidence level and is interpreted as a reliable change.

source_guidance.title: How should I interpret a large gap between the child-rated ChOCI-R-S and the parent-rated ChOCI-R-P?
source_guidance.text: Discrepancies between informants are common and the gap itself is useful clinical data. Parents typically have better visibility of observable compulsions (washing, checking, asking for reassurance) and tend to underestimate obsessions and covert rituals. Children may underreport when symptoms feel shameful, when insight is limited (more common in younger children), or when they have learned to mask symptoms in front of caregivers. When the parent score substantially exceeds the child score, consider limited insight, minimisation, or symptom concealment. When the child score exceeds the parent score, suspect covert symptoms or content the child has not disclosed at home. Both perspectives can provide valuable clinical information; the divergence becomes a formulation discussion point and may warrant exploring family accommodation patterns.

source_guidance.title: How should I respond clinically when a young person with elevated ChOCI-R-S scores also presents with anxiety, tics, or attentional difficulties?
source_guidance.text: Co-occurring psychiatric conditions are common in paediatric OCD rather than the exception, with around 74 percent of children meeting criteria for at least one additional disorder (Stiede et al., 2024). Practically, an elevated ChOCI-R-S should prompt considerations of assessment for generalised anxiety, separation anxiety, specific phobias, tic disorders, and ADHD as clinically indicated before finalising a treatment plan. Comorbidity influences sequencing: co-occurring anxiety may require adaptations to treatment planning, tic disorders can blur the line between compulsions and motor/vocal tics on the Compulsion subscale (worth clarifying in interview), and untreated ADHD can undermine engagement with between-session exposure tasks. Documenting which conditions are present, which are driving impairment, and which are likely to interact with CBT-with-ERP is more useful than ChOCI-R-S scores alone.

source_guidance.title: Does a low score or a "Minimal" descriptor mean the young person does not have OCD?
source_guidance.text: No. Because the reference sample was made up entirely of young people diagnosed with OCD, scores describe severity relative to that group rather than to the general population. A low percentile or a “Minimal” descriptor therefore means the young person’s reported symptoms or impairment are lower than those of most young people in the OCD clinical reference sample. The measure should not be used to rule OCD in or out.

source_guidance.title: With six scores produced, which should be the main focus for reporting and progress monitoring?
source_guidance.text: Total Impairment is the primary score for most purposes. It reflects overall OCD-related functional disruption and is comparable to the total score of the clinician-administered CY-BOCS, which makes it a useful headline figure and a key metric for tracking progress over the course of treatment. Total Symptoms complements it by capturing the breadth of symptoms endorsed, while the four subscale scores are best used to examine the balance of obsessions and compulsions and identify domain-specific patterns that may be obscured by the total scores.

context_sections.title: Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Child Self Report (ChOCI-R-S)
context_sections.text:
The Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) is a 38-item self-report measure of obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) symptoms (Uher et al., 2008) in children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. It is completed by the child or adolescent and measures both the obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviours they experience and the impairment these cause in daily life. There is also a parent-report version of the ChOCI ( ChOCI-R-P ) that can be completed by a parent or caregiver.
Administer Now
6 minutes
Ages 7 to 17 years
Adolescent , Child , Diagnosis , OCD

Documenting which conditions are present, which are driving impairment, and which are likely to interact with CBT-with-ERP is more useful than ChOCI-R-S scores alone.

context_sections.title: Can the ChOCI-R-S be used outside the 7 to 17 year age range?
context_sections.text: The ChOCI-R-S is intended for children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. Use below age 7 is not recommended, as percentile interpretation may be less reliable because the reference distribution does not include this end of the range, and younger children may find a self-report questionnaire hard to complete; the parent-report ChOCI-R-P is a useful alternative. Above age 17, an adult OCD measure such as the OCI-R would typically be more appropriate.

context_sections.title: How do I use repeat ChOCI-R-S administration to inform session-by-session treatment decisions?
context_sections.text: For active CBT-with-ERP, ChOCI-R-S administration every week or two may help monitor symptom and impairment changes over time. A declining Compulsion Symptoms score alongside persistently elevated Obsession Symptoms may warrant exploring whether overt rituals are reducing while the underlying obsessional content remains distressing. This suggests the exposure hierarchy may need to shift toward the feared thought rather than the behaviour. A flat or rising Impairment score despite falling Symptoms scores may indicate entrenched family accommodation that has not yet been targeted. Plateaus across several weeks may prompt a hierarchy review and a check on between-session exposure adherence. In maintenance or follow-up, administration frequency can be adjusted according to clinical need, treatment goals, and risk of symptom recurrence.

context_sections.title: Can the ChOCI-R-S be used to screen for or confirm a diagnosis of OCD?
context_sections.text: No. The ChOCI-R-S measures OCD symptom content and severity; it is not a diagnostic or screening instrument. It is intended for young people with known or suspected OCD, and its scores are referenced against an OCD-diagnosed sample rather than the general population. Diagnosis should rest on clinical assessment, and where the aim is to detect possible OCD in an unselected group, a dedicated screening measure is more appropriate.

context_sections.title: Does a low score or a "Minimal" descriptor mean the young person does not have OCD?
context_sections.text: No. Because the reference sample was made up entirely of young people diagnosed with OCD, scores describe severity relative to that group rather than to the general population. A low percentile or a “Minimal” descriptor therefore means the young person’s reported symptoms or impairment are lower than those of most young people in the OCD clinical reference sample. The measure should not be used to rule OCD in or out.

context_sections.title: With six scores produced, which should be the main focus for reporting and progress monitoring?
context_sections.text: Total Impairment is the primary score for most purposes. Total Symptoms complements it by capturing the breadth of symptoms endorsed, while the four subscale scores are best used to examine the balance of obsessions and compulsions and identify domain-specific patterns that may be obscured by the total scores.

context_sections.title: Understanding OCD in Young People
context_sections.text:
According to the DSM-5-TR, OCD is defined by two core features: obsessions and compulsions (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). Obsessions are recurrent, unwanted intrusive thoughts or images that cause anxiety or distress; compulsions are repetitive behaviours or mental acts performed to relieve that distress. Common compulsions in children and adolescents include washing, checking, reassurance-seeking, and ordering, counting or repeating until things feel “just right”; common obsessions include thoughts about accidents, death, harm coming to family, doubt, and fears of being bad or upsetting God. These are the symptoms the ChOCI-R-S asks about (Uher et al., 2008). Left untreated, paediatric OCD may disrupt school, friendships and family life and tends to persist into adulthood (Heyman et al., 2006).
Insight typically develops with age. Younger children in particular may have limited or variable awareness of their OCD symptoms, and may not be able to articulate the obsession behind a ritual. Comorbid conditions are also common in paediatric OCD and can complicate assessment, as overlapping symptoms make it harder to attribute presentations to OCD specifically (Stiede et al., 2024). Family members may accommodate OCD symptoms, which can mask how often rituals occur and how much time they take. The parent-report version (ChOCI-R-P) captures this observer perspective, complementing the self-report’s fuller access to the young person’s internal experience.

context_sections.title: Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) Dimensions
context_sections.text:
The ChOCI-R-S comprises six scored outputs across two construct dimensions:
Total Symptoms combines compulsion and obsession symptom scores to reflect the overall complexity and pervasiveness of OCD symptomatology Compulsion Symptoms measures the presence and range of common compulsive behaviours such as hand-washing, checking, ordering, counting, and reassurance-seeking Obsession Symptoms measures the presence and range of common intrusive thoughts, including thoughts of harm, doubt, death, religious or blasphemous thoughts, and aggressive or immoral content
Total Impairment combines the two impairment subscales to reflect overall OCD-related functional disruption, and is designed to be comparable to the clinician-rated CY-BOCS total. Compulsion Impairment measures the functional disruption associated with compulsions, including time spent, interference with school and friendships, distress, resistance, control, and avoidance Obsession Impairment measures the equivalent functional disruption associated with obsessions
Example ChOCI-R-S Item

context_sections.title: Clinical Application of the ChOCI-R-S
context_sections.text:
The ChOCI-R-S is designed for use with children and adolescents who have an established or suspected diagnosis of OCD. Its main uses fall into three areas:
Assessment and progress monitoring. At baseline, it quantifies symptom breadth and functional impairment to establish OCD severity. Its primary application is progress monitoring during treatment for paediatric OCD, where pre-treatment, mid-treatment and post-treatment scores can be compared to track symptom reduction and functional improvement.
Guiding formulation and treatment focus. The subscale structure can guide where a clinician focuses exposure hierarchies and cognitive intervention. The symptom and impairment profile contributes to a broader case conceptualisation alongside diagnostic interview.
Combining self- and parent-report. Pairing the self-report with the parent-report version (ChOCI-R-P) provides a more comprehensive assessment than either informant alone. A parent adds an observer’s view of how often rituals occur and how much time they take up, which a young person may minimise or not think to mention. Where the two accounts differ, that gap is often the most useful part: it can flag symptoms the young person under-reports, or point to differences in insight and how much the family is accommodating the OCD.

context_sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Severity / Descriptor Categories
context_sections.text:
Each of the six scores is reported with a severity descriptor alongside its percentile.
Symptoms: A Low label (green) indicates a symptom level lower than typical for young people with OCD (atypically light for this reference group); Moderate (yellow) indicates a symptom level within the typical range for young people with OCD; High (red) indicates a symptom level above the typical OCD-clinical range. Each subscale has its own cut-offs, placed at the same position in the reference sample as the Total Symptoms cut-offs:
Total Symptoms : Low 0–9, Moderate 10–25, High 26–40
Compulsion Symptoms : Low 0–5, Moderate 6–13, High 14–20
Obsession Symptoms : Low 0–2, Moderate 3–13, High 14–20
Impairment: A Minimal label (white) indicates functional disruption lower than typical for young people with OCD; Mild (green) indicates mild functional disruption relative to the OCD-clinical reference; Moderate (yellow) indicates functional disruption within the typical OCD-clinical range; Severe (orange) indicates functional disruption in the middle-to-upper portion of the OCD-clinical reference distribution; Extreme (red) indicates functional disruption among the highest levels observed in the OCD-clinical reference distribution. Each subscale has its own cut-offs, placed at the same position in the reference sample as the Total Impairment cut-offs:
Total Impairment : Minimal 0–9, Mild 10–19, Moderate 20–29, Severe 30–39, Extreme 40–48
Compulsion Impairment : Minimal 0–5, Mild 6–10, Moderate 11–15, Severe 16–20, Extreme 21–24
Obsession Impairment : Minimal 0–2, Mild 3–8, Moderate 9–14, Severe 15–20, Extreme 21–24

context_sections.title: Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) Development
context_sections.text:
The ChOCI-R has self-report and parent-report forms, developed and validated together (Uher et al., 2008); NovoPsych refers to them as the ChOCI-R-S and ChOCI-R-P, and ‘ChOCI-R’ below refers to the instrument as a whole or to findings covering both forms.
The ChOCI-R is a revision of the original CHOCI (Shafran et al., 2003), refined to improve item-level psychometrics and broaden severity coverage. The original CHOCI used 19 symptom items rated on a three-point scale (1 to 3) and a 10-item impairment scale derived from the CY-BOCS interview (Goodman et al., 1989; Scahill et al., 1997), scored 0 to 4. The CHOCI-R retains the 10 best-performing symptom items per section (compulsions and obsessions), changes the symptom response format to a three-option scale scored 0 to 2, and adds an avoidance item to each impairment section to align with the adult Y-BOCS. The remaining five impairment items (time, interference, distress, resistance, control) are unchanged between the original CHOCI and the ChOCI-R (Uher et al., 2008).
Published reports describe the ChOCI-R-S as a 32-item measure (the scored items only). NovoPsych’s version also administers six unscored open-text items in which the young person describes their most upsetting habits and thoughts in their own words, which, like the Y-BOCS symptom checklist, capture specific symptom content to aid formulation, giving 38 items in total.
Psychometric validation of the ChOCI-R was conducted in a sample of 285 children and adolescents attending an OCD clinic over the period 2000 to 2006 (Uher et al., 2008). All children met ICD-10 criteria for OCD established via structured clinical interview.

context_sections.title: Factor Structure of the ChOCI-R-S
context_sections.text: Formal factor analysis was conducted on the 12 impairment items, which underpin the measure’s severity scoring; the symptom items were evaluated using internal consistency rather than factor analysis (Uher et al., 2008). For the self-report version, a single common factor explained 46% of the variance in the impairment items, largely because the two resistance items loaded poorly; removing them increased the explained variance to 53%. Exploratory factor analysis further supported separate Obsession and Compulsion dimensions, with the resistance items forming a distinct factor. Consistent with this structure, NovoPsych reports separate Compulsion and Obsession scores at both the Symptoms and Impairment levels, while retaining the resistance items for clinical coverage.

context_sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Reliability
context_sections.text: Internal consistency of the ChOCI-R-S was good across the four subscales and two totals (Uher et al., 2008). For the impairment scales, Cronbach’s alpha was .82 (Obsessions Impairment, N = 249), .76 (Compulsions Impairment, N = 278) and .86 (Total Impairment, N = 244). For the symptom scales, alpha was .86 (Obsession Symptoms, N = 258), .72 (Compulsion Symptoms, N = 261) and .84 (Total Symptoms, N = 257). The lower alpha for the Compulsion Symptoms scale reflects the heterogeneity of compulsive behaviours (washing, checking, ordering, counting), which need not co-occur within a child. On the impairment scales, the two resistance items had low item-total correlations; with them removed, alpha rose to .86 (obsessions), .80 (compulsions) and .88 (total).

context_sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Validity
context_sections.text:
Convergent validity was demonstrated through moderate correlation between the ChOCI-R-S Total Impairment and the CY-BOCS Total score ( r = 0.55, N = 211, p < .001; Uher et al., 2008). This was numerically higher than the correlation for the parent-report version ( r = 0.45), although the difference between the two was not statistically significant.
Evidence for divergent validity is more mixed. Across the self- and parent-report versions, ChOCI-R severity scores correlated moderately with the SDQ emotional-problems subscale ( r = 0.30–0.51), weakly with conduct problems ( r = 0.11–0.22) and intermediately with hyperactivity ( r = 0.26–0.32) (Uher et al., 2008). Rapp and colleagues (2016) rated divergent validity as good from externalising problems but only fair to poor from emotional disorders. For the original ChOCI, sensitivity (88%) and specificity (95%) against non-clinical controls were high, but these have not been examined for the revised measure (Rapp et al., 2016).
Agreement between ChOCI-R-S and ChOCI-R-P was strong, with intraclass correlation coefficients of 0.77 (95% CI 0.69–0.83) for Total Impairment, 0.70 (95% CI 0.59–0.77) for Obsessions Impairment, and 0.80 (95% CI 0.74–0.85) for Compulsions Impairment (Uher et al., 2008).

context_sections.title: Sensitivity to Change for the ChOCI-R-S
context_sections.text: The best available data on the ChOCI-R-S’s sensitivity to change come from Lenhard and colleagues (2017), a randomised trial of internet-delivered CBT in adolescents aged 12 to 17 ( N = 67) in which the ChOCI-R-S was a secondary outcome. It reported a within-group pre-post effect of d = 0.57 (95% CI 0.16–0.98) and a between-group effect of d = 0.64 (95% CI 0.11–1.16) favouring internet-delivered CBT over waitlist ( p = .014), with continued improvement to a 3-month follow-up. This is encouraging but preliminary: a single trial, in adolescents only.

context_sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Change Score Interpretation
context_sections.text: When the ChOCI-R-S is administered on multiple occasions, change between administrations is interpreted via a Reliable Change Index (RCI) computed with the Jacobson-Truax formula, using the Uher and colleagues (2008) self-report internal consistency reliability and standard deviation for each total. A change of approximately 9.0 raw-score points or greater on Total Impairment (alpha = .86, SD = 8.7), or 8.6 or greater on Total Symptoms (alpha = .84, SD = 7.8), exceeds measurement error at the 95% confidence level and is interpreted as a reliable change.

context_sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Sample Data
context_sections.text: Reference percentiles are derived from Uher and colleagues (2008): 285 consecutive referrals (244 to 278 with complete self-report data per subscale) to an OCD clinic between 2000 and 2006, all meeting ICD-10 criteria for OCD via structured clinical interview, with no significant sex differences (boys’ age M = 13.7, range 7 to 18; girls’ age M = 13.7, range 9 to 18). Reference parameters for the self-report subscales are: Compulsion Symptoms M = 9.5, SD = 4.3; Obsession Symptoms M = 8.0, SD = 5.1; Total Symptoms M = 17.6, SD = 7.8; Compulsion Impairment M = 15.0, SD = 4.5; Obsession Impairment M = 13.5, SD = 5.2; Total Impairment M = 28.5, SD = 8.7. Because this reference sample is clinical (not community), percentile interpretation is positional within an OCD-diagnosed reference group: a percentile of 50 reflects the average level for a young person diagnosed with OCD, not the general population. No community-sample reference data exists for the self-report ChOCI-R-S, and the original authors note that confirmation in primary care and population-based samples remains needed (Uher et al., 2008).

context_sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Severity Descriptors
context_sections.text:
Each score is reported with a severity descriptor. The Total Impairment descriptors use the CY-BOCS severity bands (Goodman et al., 1989), converted to ChOCI-R-S scores using the table of equivalent scores in Uher et al. (2008). The Total Symptoms descriptors sit one standard deviation either side of the clinical mean in the same study. The lowest impairment band, called “subclinical” on the CY-BOCS, is labelled “Minimal” in NovoPsych because the reference sample is children and adolescents attending an OCD clinic.
The descriptors are a descriptive guide, not diagnostic cut-offs, and do not replace clinical judgement. NovoPsych placed each subscale’s cut-offs at the same percentile as the matching Total cut-off, using each subscale’s own mean and SD from Uher et al. (2008), with each band starting at the next whole score. For symptoms, Moderate starts at about the 16th percentile and High at about the 84th. For impairment, Mild starts at about the 1st–2nd percentile, Moderate about the 16th, Severe about the 56th and Extreme about the 90th. The parent-report ChOCI-R-P has different raw-score cut-offs, because each form is converted through its own column of the equivalence table and its own norms, so the same raw score does not mean the same thing on the two forms.
Note. The CY-BOCS severity bands (0–7, 8–15, 16–23, 24–31, 32–40) are widely used and are usually cited to Goodman et al. (1989), and sometimes to the CY-BOCS validation paper (Scahill et al., 1997). NovoPsych could not find them in either paper, in the scale authors’ later work, or anywhere else. We therefore treat them as an established clinical convention, and keep them for consistency with common practice and with earlier NovoPsych reports.

context_sections.title: Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Child Self Report (ChOCI-R-S)
context_sections.text:
The Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) is a 38-item self-report measure of obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) symptoms (Uher et al., 2008) in children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. It is completed by the child or adolescent and measures both the obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviours they experience and the impairment these cause in daily life. There is also a parent-report version of the ChOCI ( ChOCI-R-P ) that can be completed by a parent or caregiver.

context_sections.title: Understanding OCD in Young People
context_sections.text:
According to the DSM-5-TR, OCD is defined by two core features: obsessions and compulsions (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). Obsessions are recurrent, unwanted intrusive thoughts or images that cause anxiety or distress; compulsions are repetitive behaviours or mental acts performed to relieve that distress. Common compulsions in children and adolescents include washing, checking, reassurance-seeking, and ordering, counting or repeating until things feel “just right”; common obsessions include thoughts about accidents, death, harm coming to family, doubt, and fears of being bad or upsetting God. These are the symptoms the ChOCI-R-S asks about (Uher et al., 2008). Left untreated, paediatric OCD may disrupt school, friendships and family life and tends to persist into adulthood (Heyman et al., 2006).
Insight typically develops with age. Younger children in particular may have limited or variable awareness of their OCD symptoms, and may not be able to articulate the obsession behind a ritual. Comorbid conditions are also common in paediatric OCD and can complicate assessment, as overlapping symptoms make it harder to attribute presentations to OCD specifically (Stiede et al., 2024). Family members may accommodate OCD symptoms, which can mask how often rituals occur and how much time they take. The parent-report version (ChOCI-R-P) captures this observer perspective, complementing the self-report’s fuller access to the young person’s internal experience.

context_sections.title: Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) Dimensions
context_sections.text:
The ChOCI-R-S comprises six scored outputs across two construct dimensions:
Total Symptoms combines compulsion and obsession symptom scores to reflect the overall complexity and pervasiveness of OCD symptomatology Compulsion Symptoms measures the presence and range of common compulsive behaviours such as hand-washing, checking, ordering, counting, and reassurance-seeking Obsession Symptoms measures the presence and range of common intrusive thoughts, including thoughts of harm, doubt, death, religious or blasphemous thoughts, and aggressive or immoral content
Total Impairment combines the two impairment subscales to reflect overall OCD-related functional disruption, and is designed to be comparable to the clinician-rated CY-BOCS total. Compulsion Impairment measures the functional disruption associated with compulsions, including time spent, interference with school and friendships, distress, resistance, control, and avoidance Obsession Impairment measures the equivalent functional disruption associated with obsessions
Example ChOCI-R-S Item

context_sections.title: Clinical Application of the ChOCI-R-S
context_sections.text:
The ChOCI-R-S is designed for use with children and adolescents who have an established or suspected diagnosis of OCD. Its main uses fall into three areas:
Assessment and progress monitoring. At baseline, it quantifies symptom breadth and functional impairment to establish OCD severity. Its primary application is progress monitoring during treatment for paediatric OCD, where pre-treatment, mid-treatment and post-treatment scores can be compared to track symptom reduction and functional improvement.
Guiding formulation and treatment focus. The subscale structure can guide where a clinician focuses exposure hierarchies and cognitive intervention. The symptom and impairment profile contributes to a broader case conceptualisation alongside diagnostic interview.
Combining self- and parent-report. Pairing the self-report with the parent-report version (ChOCI-R-P) provides a more comprehensive assessment than either informant alone. A parent adds an observer’s view of how often rituals occur and how much time they take up, which a young person may minimise or not think to mention. Where the two accounts differ, that gap is often the most useful part: it can flag symptoms the young person under-reports, or point to differences in insight and how much the family is accommodating the OCD.

context_sections.title: Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) Scoring
context_sections.text:
The Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory–Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) produces six raw scores by summing item responses. Higher scores indicate more obsessive-compulsive symptoms or greater associated functional impairment. The ChOCI-R-S measures both symptoms and impairment:
Total Symptoms (sum of Compulsion Symptoms and Obsession Symptoms; scores range from 0 to 40) Compulsion Symptoms (items 1 to 10; scores range from 0 to 20): sum of 10 items Obsession Symptoms (items 20 to 29; scores range from 0 to 20): sum of 10 items
Total Impairment (sum of Compulsion Impairment and Obsession Impairment; scores range from 0 to 48) Compulsion Impairment (items 14 to 19; scores range from 0 to 24): sum of 6 items Obsession Impairment (items 33 to 38; scores range from 0 to 24): sum of 6 items
Six open-text items (items 11 to 13 for habits and items 30 to 32 for thoughts) ask the young person to describe their three most upsetting habits (compulsions) and thoughts (obsessions), respectively. These items are not included in the scoring, but provide additional clinical information to inform assessment and treatment planning.

context_sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Percentiles
context_sections.text: Each raw score is presented with a percentile rank against an OCD-clinical reference sample. A percentile of 50 corresponds to the OCD-clinical reference average; a percentile of 80 indicates a score exceeding approximately 80% of young people with OCD in the reference group. Because the norms come from an OCD-diagnosed sample, a low percentile does not mean a young person does not have OCD, only that their symptoms or impairment are milder than most others with the condition.

context_sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Severity / Descriptor Categories
context_sections.text:
Each of the six scores is reported with a severity descriptor alongside its percentile.
Symptoms: A Low label (green) indicates a symptom level lower than typical for young people with OCD (atypically light for this reference group); Moderate (yellow) indicates a symptom level within the typical range for young people with OCD; High (red) indicates a symptom level above the typical OCD-clinical range. Each subscale has its own cut-offs, placed at the same position in the reference sample as the Total Symptoms cut-offs:
Total Symptoms : Low 0–9, Moderate 10–25, High 26–40
Compulsion Symptoms : Low 0–5, Moderate 6–13, High 14–20
Obsession Symptoms : Low 0–2, Moderate 3–13, High 14–20
Impairment: A Minimal label (white) indicates functional disruption lower than typical for young people with OCD; Mild (green) indicates mild functional disruption relative to the OCD-clinical reference; Moderate (yellow) indicates functional disruption within the typical OCD-clinical range; Severe (orange) indicates functional disruption in the middle-to-upper portion of the OCD-clinical reference distribution; Extreme (red) indicates functional disruption among the highest levels observed in the OCD-clinical reference distribution. Each subscale has its own cut-offs, placed at the same position in the reference sample as the Total Impairment cut-offs:
Total Impairment : Minimal 0–9, Mild 10–19, Moderate 20–29, Severe 30–39, Extreme 40–48
Compulsion Impairment : Minimal 0–5, Mild 6–10, Moderate 11–15, Severe 16–20, Extreme 21–24
Obsession Impairment : Minimal 0–2, Mild 3–8, Moderate 9–14, Severe 15–20, Extreme 21–24

context_sections.title: Subscale interpretation of the ChOCI-R-S
context_sections.text: Each ChOCI-R-S subscale assesses a different aspect of obsessive-compulsive symptoms or associated impairment. Higher scores on Compulsion Symptoms indicate that the young person reports more frequent or more severe compulsive behaviours, such as washing, checking, ordering, counting and reassurance-seeking. Higher scores on Obsession Symptoms indicate more frequent intrusive thoughts of harm, doubt, death, religious or blasphemous content, or aggressive or immoral content. Higher scores on Compulsion Impairment indicate greater functional disruption from compulsions, including time spent, interference with school and friends, distress when prevented from acting, difficulty resisting or controlling compulsions, and avoidance. Higher scores on Obsession Impairment indicate similar impacts associated with obsessive thoughts.

context_sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Change Score Interpretation
context_sections.text: When the ChOCI-R-S is administered on multiple occasions, change between administrations can be evaluated using a Reliable Change Index (RCI). A change of approximately 9.0 raw-score points or greater on Total Impairment, or 8.6 or greater on Total Symptoms, indicates a change that is unlikely to be attributable to measurement error alone.

context_sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Graphs
context_sections.text:
On first administration, the report presents a results table followed by two construct sections (Symptoms and Impairment). Each section contains two horizontal raw-score charts. The first plots the construct’s total as a single bar with the client’s raw score on a 0–40 axis for Symptoms or 0–48 for Impairment. A clinical 25th-to-75th percentile reference rectangle and a dashed line at the clinical average show the score relative to the clinical reference sample of young people with OCD. The second plots the construct’s two subscales (Compulsion and Obsession bars on a 0–20 axis for Symptoms or 0–24 for Impairment, each with its own 25th-to-75th reference rectangle and clinical-average line). Beneath each bar, a coloured strip marks that scale’s descriptor bands (Low, Moderate and High for Symptoms; Minimal, Mild, Moderate, Severe and Extreme for Impairment, with Minimal shown in white).


On repeat administration, the report presents the same results table followed by a 2×3 grid of multi-administration raw-score line plots organised by construct: top row Symptoms (Total, Compulsions, Obsessions); bottom row Impairment (Total, Compulsions, Obsessions). Each plot shows one score over time on its own descriptor bands, so the shading behind each point matches that score’s descriptor in the results table. Unlike the first-administration charts, these graphs emphasise longitudinal change rather than position within the clinical reference distribution.

context_sections.title: Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) Development
context_sections.text:
The ChOCI-R has self-report and parent-report forms, developed and validated together (Uher et al., 2008); NovoPsych refers to them as the ChOCI-R-S and ChOCI-R-P, and ‘ChOCI-R’ below refers to the instrument as a whole or to findings covering both forms.

Psychometric validation of the ChOCI-R was conducted in a sample of 285 children and adolescents attending an OCD clinic over the period 2000 to 2006 (Uher et al., 2008). All children met ICD-10 criteria for OCD established via structured clinical interview.

context_sections.title: How should I interpret a large gap between the child-rated ChOCI-R-S and the parent-rated ChOCI-R-P?
context_sections.text: Discrepancies between informants are common and the gap itself is useful clinical data. Parents typically have better visibility of observable compulsions (washing, checking, asking for reassurance) and tend to underestimate obsessions and covert rituals. Children may underreport when symptoms feel shameful, when insight is limited (more common in younger children), or when they have learned to mask symptoms in front of caregivers. When the parent score substantially exceeds the child score, consider limited insight, minimisation, or symptom concealment. When the child score exceeds the parent score, suspect covert symptoms or content the child has not disclosed at home. Both perspectives can provide valuable clinical information; the divergence becomes a formulation discussion point and may warrant exploring family accommodation patterns.

context_sections.title: How should I respond clinically when a young person with elevated ChOCI-R-S scores also presents with anxiety, tics, or attentional difficulties?
context_sections.text: Co-occurring psychiatric conditions are common in paediatric OCD rather than the exception, with around 74 percent of children meeting criteria for at least one additional disorder (Stiede et al., 2024). Practically, an elevated ChOCI-R-S should prompt considerations of assessment for generalised anxiety, separation anxiety, specific phobias, tic disorders, and ADHD as clinically indicated before finalising a treatment plan. Comorbidity influences sequencing: co-occurring anxiety may require adaptations to treatment planning, tic disorders can blur the line between compulsions and motor/vocal tics on the Compulsion subscale (worth clarifying in interview), and untreated ADHD can undermine engagement with between-session exposure tasks. Documenting which conditions are present, which are driving impairment, and which are likely to interact with CBT-with-ERP is more useful than ChOCI-R-S scores alone.

context_sections.title: Can the ChOCI-R-S be used outside the 7 to 17 year age range?
context_sections.text: The ChOCI-R-S is intended for children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. Use below age 7 is not recommended, as percentile interpretation may be less reliable because the reference distribution does not include this end of the range, and younger children may find a self-report questionnaire hard to complete; the parent-report ChOCI-R-P is a useful alternative. Above age 17, an adult OCD measure such as the OCI-R would typically be more appropriate.

context_sections.title: How do I use repeat ChOCI-R-S administration to inform session-by-session treatment decisions?
context_sections.text: For active CBT-with-ERP, ChOCI-R-S administration every week or two may help monitor symptom and impairment changes over time. A declining Compulsion Symptoms score alongside persistently elevated Obsession Symptoms may warrant exploring whether overt rituals are reducing while the underlying obsessional content remains distressing. This suggests the exposure hierarchy may need to shift toward the feared thought rather than the behaviour. A flat or rising Impairment score despite falling Symptoms scores may indicate entrenched family accommodation that has not yet been targeted. Plateaus across several weeks may prompt a hierarchy review and a check on between-session exposure adherence. In maintenance or follow-up, administration frequency can be adjusted according to clinical need, treatment goals, and risk of symptom recurrence.

context_sections.title: Can the ChOCI-R-S be used to screen for or confirm a diagnosis of OCD?
context_sections.text: No. The ChOCI-R-S measures OCD symptom content and severity; it is not a diagnostic or screening instrument. It is intended for young people with known or suspected OCD, and its scores are referenced against an OCD-diagnosed sample rather than the general population. Diagnosis should rest on clinical assessment, and where the aim is to detect possible OCD in an unselected group, a dedicated screening measure is more appropriate.

context_sections.title: Does a low score or a "Minimal" descriptor mean the young person does not have OCD?
context_sections.text: No. Because the reference sample was made up entirely of young people diagnosed with OCD, scores describe severity relative to that group rather than to the general population. A low percentile or a “Minimal” descriptor therefore means the young person’s reported symptoms or impairment are lower than those of most young people in the OCD clinical reference sample. The measure should not be used to rule OCD in or out.

context_sections.title: With six scores produced, which should be the main focus for reporting and progress monitoring?
context_sections.text: Total Impairment is the primary score for most purposes. It reflects overall OCD-related functional disruption and is comparable to the total score of the clinician-administered CY-BOCS, which makes it a useful headline figure and a key metric for tracking progress over the course of treatment. Total Symptoms complements it by capturing the breadth of symptoms endorsed, while the four subscale scores are best used to examine the balance of obsessions and compulsions and identify domain-specific patterns that may be obscured by the total scores.

previous_source_metadata.description: The Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) is a 38-item self-report measure of obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) symptoms (Uher et al., 2008) in children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. It is completed by the child or adolescent and measures both the obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviours they experience and the impairment these cause in daily life. There is also a parent-report version of the ChOCI ( ChOCI-R-P ) that can be completed by a parent or caregiver.

Interpretation
        The self-report Children's Obsessional Compulsive Inventory–Revised (ChOCI-R-S) was
        administered on 06 November 2026.

        Symptoms: The respondent scored 22 out of a possible 40 on Total Symptoms, placing them at
        the 71st percentile. Their reported symptoms fall within the moderate range for young people
        with OCD. This reflected moderate obsessions (7/20) and high compulsions (15/20). Examples
        of endorsed items include:
        - 1. I spend far too much time washing my hands over and over again. (A lot)
        - 2. I feel I must do ordinary/everyday things exactly the same way, every time I do them. (A lot)

        Impairment: The respondent scored 25 out of a possible 48 on Total Impairment, placing them
        at the 34th percentile. Their reported functional impairment falls within the moderate range for
        young people with OCD. This reflected mild impairment from obsessions (8/24) and severe
        impairment from compulsions (17/24). Examples of endorsed items include:
        - 16. How would you feel if prevented from carrying out your habits? How upset would you
        become? (Totally)
        - 15. How much do these habits get in the way of school or doing things with friends? (A lot)

        The respondent's open-text descriptions of their habits (items 11 to 13) and thoughts (items 30
        to 32) appear in the Client Responses section and may guide formulation.


Scoring and Interpretation Information
        For comprehensive information on the ChOCI-R-S, see here.

        ChOCI-R-S Scoring
        The Children's Obsessional Compulsive Inventory–Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S)
        produces six raw scores by summing item responses. Higher scores indicate more obsessive-
        compulsive symptoms or greater associated functional impairment. The ChOCI-R-S measures
        both symptoms and impairment:
        - Total Symptoms (sum of Compulsion Symptoms and Obsession Symptoms; scores range from
        0 to 40)
        - Compulsion Symptoms (items 1 to 10; scores range from 0 to 20): sum of 10 items
        - Obsession Symptoms (items 20 to 29; scores range from 0 to 20): sum of 10 items

        - Total Impairment (sum of Compulsion Impairment and Obsession Impairment; scores range
        from 0 to 48)
        - Compulsion Impairment (items 14 to 19; scores range from 0 to 24): sum of 6 items
        - Obsession Impairment (items 33 to 38; scores range from 0 to 24): sum of 6 items

        Six open-text items (items 11 to 13 for habits and items 30 to 32 for thoughts) ask the young
